Resin Teeth Processed Directly to Metal Bases
nodes.summary: The text discusses methods of attaching artificial teeth to partial denture bases, including acrylic resin attachment, cementation to metal bases, direct processing of resin teeth to metal, metal teeth cast with the framework, and chemical bonding. It covers advantages, disadvantages, technical details, and clinical considerations for each method, including retention mechanisms, tooth selection, occlusal adjustments, and prevention of metal-resin separation. It also addresses the need for relining distal extension bases due to changes in residual ridge support, emphasizing the importance of relinable materials and the use of wax strips of known thickness rather than articulating ribbon to assess occlusal contacts.

nodes.title: NEED FOR RELINING
nodes.summary: The text covers denture base considerations for removable partial dentures, focusing on distal extension bases. It explains the need for relining due to residual ridge changes, how to detect loss of support through occlusal contact loss and rotation about the fulcrum line, and methods for evaluating these changes using wax strips and tissue-conditioning materials. It compares acrylic-resin and metal bases, noting acrylic is generally preferred because it can be relined, while metal bases may be used in selected stable ridge situations. It also discusses stress-breakers and stress equalizers, their designs, benefits, drawbacks, and the importance of rigid conventional designs. Figure captions add information on cast molar frameworks, silica coating for resin retention, wax occlusal checks, and assessment of lingual plate displacement indicating poor ridge support.

nodes.title: STRESS-BREAKERS (STRESS EQUALIZERS)
nodes.summary: The text covers removable partial denture design concepts: metal distal extension bases and replacement techniques; stress-breakers/stress equalizers, their clasp designs, benefits, and drawbacks; a clinical note on lingual plate displacement and relining; and an outline of chapter topics including the differences between tooth-supported and tooth-tissue-supported prostheses, design components, implant considerations, systematic design examples, and additional design influences. It emphasizes that tooth-supported prostheses have predictable support, while tooth-tissue-supported prostheses involve variable residual ridge support and greater design complexity.

structure.summary: This section covers denture base considerations in removable partial dentures, including the functions of denture bases, differences between tooth-supported and distal extension bases, and retention mechanisms. It describes methods for attaching acrylic-resin and metal bases, requirements for ideal denture base materials, and advantages of metal bases. It also details methods of attaching artificial teeth, the need for and evaluation of relining in distal extension bases, and the role, designs, and limitations of stress-breakers/stress equalizers.

structure.title: Principles of Removable Partial Denture Design

nodes.title: DIFFERENCE IN PROSTHESIS SUPPORT AND INFLUENCE ON DESIGN
nodes.summary: The text covers principles of removable partial denture design, focusing on the difference between tooth-supported and tooth-tissue-supported prostheses. It explains how support type affects movement, design variability, impression registration, indirect retention, and base material choice, and distinguishes between Kennedy Class I/II distal extension RPDs and Class III tooth-supported RPDs. It also notes the influence of opposing arch factors and tissue displacement on design.

nodes.title: DIFFERENTIATION BETWEEN TWO MAIN TYPES OF REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES
Differences in Support
nodes.summary: This text, from Chapter 10 on principles of removable partial denture design, discusses support and impression registration for partial dentures. It explains that tooth-supported restorations rarely need relining and often use metal bases, while distal extension bases rely on the residual ridge for support; ridge characteristics and tissue displaceability affect stability and abutment loading. It outlines the two requirements for impression registration: accurate recording of anatomic structures using elastic impression materials, and proper recording of soft-tissue support to use firm areas as primary stress-bearing regions. It also describes Figure 10-3, which shows how extension length and tissue displacement create lever action on abutments and how different ridge forms affect support and stability.

nodes.title: Impression Registration
nodes.summary: The text covers principles of removable partial denture design, focusing on differences between tooth-supported and distal extension (tooth- and tissue-supported) RPDs. It discusses support differences, impression registration requirements and materials, clasp design variations, stress dissipation, combination clasps, and factors influencing stress transfer to abutment teeth and residual ridges.

nodes.title: Differences in Clasp Design
nodes.summary: The text covers principles of removable partial denture design, focusing on differences between tooth-supported and tooth-and-tissue-supported prostheses. It discusses impression techniques for distal extension bases, clasp design requirements, stress-breaking strategies and combination clasps, factors affecting stress transfer, and a systematic framework-design approach based on support, connection, retention, and base support. It lists criteria for evaluating abutment teeth and edentulous ridge support, emphasizes equitable load distribution through rests, minor connectors, and guiding planes, and describes how design choices influence stress distribution to abutment teeth and residual ridges.

The section differentiates the two main types of removable partial dentures: tooth-supported (Kennedy Class III) and tooth- and tissue-supported distal extension types (Kennedy Class I and Class II). It covers their differences in support, tissue and abutment displacement, impression registration and jaw records, need for indirect retention, rotation behavior, and base material selection (relinable acrylic resin versus metal bases). It also addresses opposing-arch/occlusal influences on design, clasp design variations, stress-breaking and combination clasps, systematic framework design, and equitable load distribution to abutment teeth and residual ridges.

nodes.title: ESSENTIALS OF PARTIAL DENTURE DESIGN
nodes.summary: The text covers principles of removable partial denture (RPD) design, beginning with a figure showing how different minor connector/guiding plane contacts affect stress distribution to abutment teeth and the ridge. It then outlines a systematic five-step design process: determining support, connecting tooth and tissue support units, determining retention, connecting retention units to support units, and outlining/joining the edentulous area. Factors for evaluating abutment tooth support and edentulous ridge support are detailed, along with the need for rigid major connectors and properly designed minor connectors. Retention principles, clasp selection criteria, and the importance of undercut location are discussed, supported by a clinical trial showing RPI and circumferential clasp designs produced similar outcomes. The text also describes components of partial dentures, including support, connectors, and retainers, and explains special considerations for tooth and tissue-supported prostheses, such as composite support, direct-indirect retention, and minimizing distal extension base movement. Finally, tooth support is described as dependent on alveolar support, morphology, framework rigidity, and rest design, with mention of possible splinting of abutment teeth.

nodes.title: COMPONENTS OF PARTIAL DENTURE DESIGN
Tooth Support
nodes.summary: The text covers principles of removable partial denture design, emphasizing a systematic approach to connectors, retention, clasp selection, and component integration. It discusses tooth versus ridge support, especially for distal extension bases, highlighting composite support, indirect retention, and tissue response. It includes clinical evidence showing RPI and circumferential clasp designs perform similarly, and details factors affecting tooth and ridge support, abutment preparation, denture base accuracy, occlusal load reduction, and impression techniques—with functional-form impressions offering better stability than anatomic-form impressions.

nodes.title: Ridge Support
nodes.summary: The text discusses principles of removable partial denture design, emphasizing the dentist's responsibility for abutment preparation and rest seats, while the technician is accountable for casting accuracy. It explains support mechanisms for tooth-supported and distal extension RPDs, listing factors affecting tissue support, including ridge quality, impression technique, denture base accuracy, framework design, and occlusal load. It highlights the need for functional-form impressions of stress-bearing areas, wide load distribution, and the benefits of functional-form denture bases for stability. Implants are noted as a way to improve ridge support. Finally, it defines major and minor connectors and notes that a major connector should be properly located.

nodes.title: Major and Minor Connectors
nodes.summary: The text covers removable partial denture design principles: reducing occlusal load through smaller posterior teeth, obtaining functional ridge impressions with custom trays, and using implants to improve ridge support. It describes major/minor connectors and their rigidity, lingual bar and linguoplate design and indications, palatal connector options, and direct retainer requirements for both tooth-supported and distal extension partial dentures, including clasp design, avoidance of tissue impingement, stress-breaking behavior, and horizontal stabilization.

nodes.title: Direct Retainers for Tooth-Supported Partial Dentures
nodes.summary: The text discusses removable partial denture design principles, focusing on major connectors such as the lingual bar, linguoplate, and palatal connectors, including their design requirements, indications, and tissue considerations. It then covers direct retainers for tooth-supported and distal extension partial dentures, explaining their functions, acceptable types, clasp design criteria, limitations of bar clasps, and how distal extension retainers must accommodate tissue-ward movement.

nodes.title: Direct Retainers for Distal Extension Partial Dentures
nodes.summary: The text covers removable partial denture design principles, focusing on major connectors, direct retainers, and stabilizing components. It describes requirements for rigid lingual and palatal connectors, indications for linguoplate and continuous bar retainer, and design preferences for palatal connectors. It explains functions and selection of direct retainers for tooth-supported and distal extension dentures, including clasp design considerations, stress-breaking behavior, and indications for bar clasps. It also discusses stabilizing components such as minor connectors and reciprocal clasp arms, their design requirements, and a lingual-surface modification. Finally, it addresses guiding plane surfaces and their role in enhancing resistance to horizontal rotation.

nodes.title: Stabilizing Components
nodes.summary: The text discusses clasp arm flexibility for stress-breaking, emphasizing round tapered designs over bulky arms, and suitable clasp types for extension bases. It then covers stabilizing components, focusing on rigid minor connectors and reciprocal clasp arms, their design requirements, and a modified lingual minor connector variation with benefits and drawbacks. Finally, it explains guiding plane surfaces and how divergent horizontal planes improve cross-arch resistance to rotation.

nodes.title: Guiding Plane
nodes.summary: The text covers removable partial denture design principles for guiding planes and indirect retainers. Guiding planes are parallel vertical abutment surfaces that direct prosthesis placement/removal, are contacted by various framework components, and provide a single path, stability, retention, and reduced food trapping. They should be parallel to abutment long axes, placed on multiple widely separated abutments, sized about one-third buccolingual width and two-thirds crown height, and designed without line angles. Figures illustrate the proper cylindrical guiding plane shape and warn against facing guiding planes on lone standing abutments. Indirect retainers should be positioned as far anterior from the fulcrum line as support allows, on a capable abutment rest seat, and cannot function on inclined surfaces or weak incisors.

nodes.title: Indirect Retainers
nodes.summary: The text covers principles of removable partial denture design, focusing on guiding planes, indirect retainers, implant considerations, and systematic design examples. It explains the definition, components, functions, and preparation guidelines for guiding planes, as well as rules for indirect retainer placement, support, and the role of terminal rests. It also discusses how dental implants can help control prosthesis movement and improve stability, particularly in Kennedy Class I and II cases. Finally, it describes the Kennedy Class III RPD as a tooth-supported design, including clasp options, lack of need for indirect retention, and choice of metal denture bases.

The section covers the components and systematic design of removable partial dentures, including tooth and ridge support, major/minor connectors, direct retainers, stabilizing components, guiding planes, and indirect retainers. It emphasizes composite support for distal extension bases, factors affecting support, functional-form impressions, occlusal load reduction, and implants to improve support and stability. Connector design is detailed for lingual bar, linguoplate, continuous bar retainer, and palatal connectors, stressing rigidity and tissue considerations. Direct retainers are discussed for both tooth-supported and distal extension RPDs, including clasp design, bar clasp limitations, stress-breaking, and the similar clinical performance of RPI and circumferential clasps. Stabilizing components, modified lingual minor connectors, and guiding plane surfaces are described for horizontal stabilization and resistance to rotation. Guiding plane preparation and indirect retainer placement rules are given, along with implant considerations for Kennedy Class I/II and the tooth-supported Kennedy Class III design.

nodes.title: IMPLANT CONSIDERATIONS IN DESIGN
nodes.summary: The text covers two main topics: indirect retainers and implant considerations in removable partial denture (RPD) design, followed by an example of systematic design for a Kennedy Class III RPD. It explains that indirect retainers also support major connectors and prevent settling, clarifies that cingulum bars and linguoplates are not indirect retainers and need terminal rests, and discusses how implants can reduce prosthesis movement to improve tissue tolerance. It then describes Class III RPD design as tooth-supported, not requiring indirect retention or functional ridge impressions, with choices among clasp types and possible metal denture bases unless relining is expected.

nodes.title: EXAMPLES OF SYSTEMATIC APPROACH TO DESIGN
key_items: Kennedy Class I, Bilateral, Distal Extension Removable Partial Dentures
Kennedy Class II Removable Partial Dentures
nodes.summary: The text discusses principles of removable partial denture (RPD) design, covering the purposes and placement of indirect retainers, the role of implants in controlling prosthesis movement, and systematic design approaches for Kennedy Class III, Class I, and Class II RPDs. It also addresses additional design considerations including maximum use of abutment support, splint bars for replacing anterior teeth, and internal clip attachments for support and retention.

nodes.title: ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS INFLUENCING DESIGN
key_items: Use of a Splint Bar for Denture Support
Overlay Abutment as Support for a Denture Base
Use of a Component Partial to Gain Support
nodes.summary: The text discusses removable partial denture design considerations, emphasizing ways to gain maximum support from abutments and minimize load on residual ridges. It covers splint bars, internal clip attachments, overlay abutments, and component partials as support options, along with their fabrication and design details. It then introduces the chapter on surveying, describing its purposes, factors influencing path of placement, step-by-step surveying procedures, and the importance of the dental surveyor in planning successful removable prostheses.

structure.summary: The section covers the principles of removable partial denture design, emphasizing the fundamental distinction between tooth-supported (Kennedy Class III) and tooth-tissue-supported distal extension (Kennedy Class I/II) prostheses. It explains how the type of support influences prosthesis movement, impression registration, jaw records, indirect retention, rotation behavior, clasp design, and base material selection. A systematic five-step design process is presented, covering support determination, connectors, retention, minor connectors, and the edentulous area outline. Components such as major/minor connectors, direct retainers, stabilizing elements, guiding planes, and indirect retainers are described in detail. The section also discusses implant considerations, strategies to improve support and minimize ridge loading including splint bars, internal clip attachments, overlay abutments, and component partials, and introduces surveying principles and procedures essential for successful RPD planning.

structure.title: Surveying

nodes.title: DESCRIPTION OF DENTAL SURVEYOR
nodes.summary: The text discusses dental surveyors, focusing on moderately priced models sufficient for partial denture work and related procedures. It describes the Ney and Jelenko surveyors, their parts, similarities, and differences, including arm movement and vertical arm mechanisms. It covers accessory tools, the Ney surveyor's use as a drill press, mentions other surveyor types, and lists surveyor purposes such as surveying diagnostic casts and recontouring abutment teeth.

nodes.title: PURPOSES OF THE SURVEYOR
Surveying the Diagnostic Cast
nodes.summary: The text covers the uses of the surveyor's lab handpiece clamp and the essential process of surveying the diagnostic cast for removable partial denture planning. It details the objectives of surveying, including determining the path of placement/removal, identifying guiding planes, locating retention, avoiding interference, optimizing esthetics, charting preparations, marking heights of contour/undercuts, and recording cast orientation. It also describes using undercut gauges and the surveyor blade to measure and trim stone casts as a blueprint for intraoral tooth reduction, and contouring wax patterns with the surveyor blade to maintain the selected path of placement for abutment restorations.

nodes.title: Contouring Wax Patterns
nodes.summary: The text describes the use of the dental surveyor in treatment planning and mouth preparation, including contouring abutment teeth and wax patterns, recording cast orientation, surveying ceramic veneer crowns, placing intracoronal retainers/internal attachments, and preparing internal rest seats. It emphasizes maintaining the planned path of placement, achieving proper guide planes, retentive undercuts, and esthetic/functional contours, with final adjustments made before glazing or casting.

nodes.title: Surveying Crowns, Intracoronal Retainers, and Internal Rest Seats
nodes.summary: The page covers surveying procedures for ceramic veneer crowns and placement of intracoronal retainers and internal rest seats. It emphasizes proper contouring for clasp placement, use of the surveyor to verify and adjust veneered crowns before final glaze, a stepwise method for placing intracoronal attachments with parallel keyways, and the use of the surveyor as a drill press for internal rest seats, including their functional advantages and torque considerations.

nodes.title: Placement of Internal Rest Seats
nodes.summary: The text describes the use of the dental surveyor in fixed and removable prosthodontics. It covers contouring restorations for clasp placement, surveying and finishing ceramic veneer crowns before final glaze, and using the surveyor for intracoronal retainers and internal rest seats. It explains the difference between internal rests and attachments, indications and contraindications of interlocking rests, and how to machine cast restorations for parallel guiding planes. Finally, it details surveying the master cast: selecting the path of placement, measuring retention, blockout of undesirable undercuts, and preparing the master cast with wax relief and blockout.

nodes.title: Machining Cast Restorations
nodes.summary: The text covers rest selection and internal rest seat preparation for partial dentures, machining of cast restorations to achieve parallel guiding planes, and surveying the master cast. It emphasizes using proper rest designs for distal extension cases, preparing internal rest boxes with appropriate burs, machining cast surfaces with carborundum points and indexes when needed, and the objectives of master cast surveying: selecting the path of placement, measuring retention relative to clasp flexibility and undercuts, locating and blocking out undesirable undercuts, and trimming blockout parallel to the path of insertion. It also describes modifying master casts with wax relief and blockout wax, as illustrated by examples on specific teeth.

nodes.title: Surveying the Master Cast
nodes.summary: The text covers principles of surveying and path of placement for removable partial dentures, including rest seat design for distal extension cases, machining of cast restorations to achieve parallel guiding planes, surveying the master cast to select the path of placement and manage blockout/relief, and the four key factors determining path of placement and removal: guiding planes, retentive areas, interference, and esthetics. It emphasizes design goals of avoiding abutment strain, ensuring easy insertion/removal, adequate retention, and acceptable appearance, while prioritizing tissue preservation.

The section covers the purposes and applications of the dental surveyor in removable partial denture planning and prosthodontic treatment. It describes surveyor tools, the Ney surveyor's use as a drill press, and notes that more elaborate surveyors offer little advantage. It details surveying the diagnostic cast to establish the path of placement/removal, guiding planes, retention, interferences, and esthetics, and to record cast orientation and undercuts. It also covers contouring wax patterns and abutment teeth, surveying ceramic veneer crowns before glazing, and placing intracoronal retainers/internal attachments with parallel keyways and internal rest seats. The section explains machining cast restorations for parallel guiding planes, rest design for distal extension cases, and internal rest versus attachment distinctions, including interlocking rest indications and torque. Finally, it addresses surveying the master cast: selecting the path of placement, measuring retention, blocking out undesirable undercuts, and applying wax relief and blockout, emphasizing the four determinants of the path—guiding planes, retentive areas, interference, and esthetics—while prioritizing tissue preservation, ease of insertion/removal, adequate retention, and acceptable appearance.

nodes.title: FACTORS THAT DETERMINE PATH OF PLACEMENT AND REMOVAL
nodes.summary: The text explains partial denture design requirements, focusing on avoiding abutment strain, easy patient insertion/removal, adequate retention, and acceptable esthetics. It identifies four factors determining the path of placement and removal: guiding planes, retentive areas, interference, and esthetics, describing how each affects prosthesis function and preparation. It then outlines step-by-step surveyor procedures, including attaching the diagnostic cast, orienting the occlusal plane, and assessing proximal surfaces to establish guiding planes.

nodes.title: STEP-BY-STEP PROCEDURES IN SURVEYING A DIAGNOSTIC CAST
Guiding Planes
nodes.summary: The text describes surveying procedures for removable partial dentures, emphasizing path of insertion considerations for anterior tooth replacement and minimizing tooth alteration. It details the recommended surveyor handling technique, step-by-step surveying of a diagnostic cast, establishment of guiding planes through anteroposterior and lateral tilting, and evaluation of retentive areas based on abutment classification and cervical convergence. The desired cast orientation provides parallel guiding planes and uniform retention but necessarily requires some tooth modification, with interference evaluation deferred.

nodes.title: Retentive Areas
nodes.summary: The text explains how to select anteroposterior and lateral tilt of a cast on a dental surveyor to establish guiding planes and balance retention. Proximal surface parallelism guides anteroposterior tilt; marginal ridge contact is preferred over cervical-only contact and may allow recontouring, while restoration is needed if proximal contact is absent. Lateral tilt is considered to distribute retentive areas on principal abutments, with guidance based on Kennedy Class configurations and an exception for poor-prognosis abutments. The final tilted position should enable parallel guiding planes and acceptable retention, generally requiring tooth modification; interference with the tentative path of placement has not yet been evaluated.

nodes.title: Interference
nodes.summary: The text discusses interference during surveying and treatment planning for removable partial dentures, focusing on the mandibular and maxillary arches, major connectors, denture bases, minor connectors, and clasp arms. It outlines causes of interference, options such as altering the path of placement, surgical or tooth recontouring, and design changes, while emphasizing preservation of guiding planes, retention, and denture base support. It also covers proper placement of clasp arms, commonly overlooked interferences at premolar and molar line angles, management of high or severe retentive undercuts, and the importance of esthetics in the final path of placement.

nodes.title: Esthetics
nodes.summary: The text covers surveying in removable partial denture treatment planning, focusing on interference identification and management for major connectors, denture bases, minor connectors, and clasp arms; esthetic considerations in clasp and tooth placement; selection of the final path of placement balancing guiding planes, retention, interference, and esthetics; and systematic documentation on diagnostic casts and treatment plans, including red markings, denture design sketches, mouth preparation sequencing, and record-keeping.

This section covers step-by-step diagnostic cast surveying for removable partial dentures. It describes establishing guiding planes and evaluating retentive areas through anteroposterior and lateral cast tilting, balancing retention among abutments, and achieving parallel guiding planes with acceptable tooth modification. It also addresses identifying and managing interferences related to major connectors, denture bases, minor connectors, and clasp arms, including options such as altering the path of placement, recontouring, or design changes. Esthetic considerations and the final choice of path of placement are discussed, along with systematic documentation of findings, denture design, and mouth preparation on diagnostic casts and treatment records.

nodes.title: FINAL PATH OF PLACEMENT
nodes.summary: The text discusses how clasp design and esthetics influence the path of placement, with esthetics considered alongside mechanical factors and prioritized for anterior replacements. The final path of placement balances guiding planes, retention, interference, and esthetics. Mouth preparations are marked in red on diagnostic casts, with extractions/surgery prioritized and rest seats deferred until later. A tentative denture design is sketched after the path is chosen, and a complete treatment plan is documented on casts, charts, and fee records. Surveyor-guided trimming of stone teeth shows the location and plane of required tooth reduction. Finally, methods for recording the cast-surveyor relationship, including tripoding and scoring the cast base, ensure the original path of placement can be reestablished for future work.

nodes.title: RECORDING RELATION OF CAST TO SURVEYOR
nodes.summary: The text describes surveying procedures in removable partial denture planning: preparing guiding planes, recording and reestablishing the cast-to-surveyor relationship using tripoding or base scoring, surveying the master cast to determine tilt and balanced retention, marking heights of contour with carbon markers, avoiding worn instruments, and measuring retentive undercuts with gauges to guide blockout and clasp placement.

nodes.title: SURVEYING THE MASTER CAST
nodes.summary: The text covers methods for preserving and repositioning cast orientation on a surveyor, including tripoding or scoring reference lines, and warns about reorientation error and losing marks. It describes surveying the master cast to establish proper tilt and guiding planes, achieve balanced retention, and manage blockout. It also covers marking heights of contour with carbon markers, avoiding worn markers, and measuring retentive undercuts with undercut gauges, noting that 0.01 inch is often adequate for cast retainers. The text ends with an incomplete fragment.

nodes.title: MEASURING RETENTION
nodes.summary: This text describes procedures for preserving cast orientation, surveying the master cast, measuring retention, and blocking out for removable partial denture frameworks. Orientation is maintained by tripod pits or scored base lines, which transfer to duplicate/refractory casts; reorientation has about 0.2 mm error and must be done carefully. The master cast is surveyed using guiding planes for anteroposterior tilt and lateral tilt for balanced retention, with clasp flexibility and undercut considerations. Carbon markers mark heights of contour and interferences, and worn markers must be discarded. Undercut gauges measure retention depths, with typical values of 0.01 inch for cast retainers and 0.02 inch for long wrought-wire arms; 0.03 inch is rarely justified. Retention depends on cervical convergence, clasp-terminal depth, and clasp flexibility. Final designs are marked with crayon pencil. Blockout removes undercuts crossed by rigid framework parts, using paralleled surveyor-trimmed hard inlay wax for guiding-plane/connector areas and arbitrary hard baseplate wax or oil clay for non-involved areas; water-soluble clay is avoided. The technician must trim blockout sufficiently to expose guiding-plane surfaces.

nodes.title: BLOCKING OUT THE MASTER CAST
nodes.summary: The text covers surveying-related procedures for master casts in removable partial denture fabrication, including the placement and duplication of wax ledges for clasp patterns, the definition and purposes of blockout, materials and methods for blockout, the distinction between blockout and relief, and considerations for lingual bar rotation and tissue impingement. It also describes illustrated examples of parallel blockout and relief on casts and the importance of accurate technician work to preserve guiding planes and ensure proper framework seating.

nodes.title: RELIEVING THE MASTER CAST
nodes.summary: The text discusses the processes of blockout and relief on master casts for removable partial denture frameworks, emphasizing the distinction between them. It details how parallel blockout and relief prevent tissue trauma, ensure proper framework seating, and accommodate denture base material. Specific guidance is given for lingual bar connectors, including managing vertical and horizontal rotational forces, selecting appropriate waxes for relief, and avoiding impingement. It also addresses relief over gingival areas and crevices, and notes that a table differentiates paralleled blockout, shaped blockout, arbitrary blockout, and relief, with special considerations for palatal major connectors.

nodes.title: PARALLELED BLOCKOUT, SHAPED BLOCKOUT, ARBITRARY BLOCKOUT, AND RELIEF
key_items: Parallel Blockout; Shaped Blockout; Arbitrary Blockout
nodes.summary: The text covers dental survey/blockout and relief procedures for mandibular removable partial denture frameworks, emphasizing how lingual bars interact with the lingual alveolar ridge, the need for parallel blockout and additional wax relief to prevent impingement, materials and techniques for blockout/relief, and the differentiation among paralleled blockout, shaped blockout, arbitrary blockout, and relief. It then transitions to a new chapter on diagnosis and treatment planning, outlining its contents and beginning with the purpose and uniqueness of prosthodontic treatment, the four-step treatment process, and the initial patient interview concept.

structure.summary: The section covers the dental surveyor's definition, components, and uses in removable partial denture planning and fabrication. It explains the purposes of surveying, including diagnostic cast analysis, wax pattern contouring, ceramic veneer crown evaluation, placement of intracoronal retainers and internal rest seats, machining cast restorations, and master cast surveying. It details the four factors determining the path of placement and removal—guiding planes, retentive areas, interference, and esthetics—and provides step-by-step procedures for surveying a diagnostic cast, selecting the final path, and recording the cast-surveyor relationship. It also describes surveying and measuring retention on the master cast, blocking out and relieving the master cast, and distinguishing paralleled blockout, shaped blockout, arbitrary blockout, and relief. Throughout, emphasis is placed on proper path selection, balanced retention, prevention of tissue impingement, accurate reorientation, and precise laboratory procedures to ensure a well-fitting removable partial denture.

structure.title: Diagnosis and Treatment Planning

nodes.title: Summary
nodes.summary: The text is the opening of Chapter 12 on diagnosis and treatment planning. It lists the chapter's topics—from patient interview, shared decision making, clinical examination, diagnostic casts, and interpretation of data through infection control, fixed versus removable partial dentures, denture choices, and metal alloy selection—then explains that dental treatment must address both the patient's perceived concerns and clinically identified needs. Each partially edentulous patient is unique, and treatment planning involves four steps: interviewing to understand the complaint/history, examining to determine needs, creating an individualized plan considering medical/oral conditions, and executing sequenced treatment with follow-up. The best care can range from no treatment to extensive treatment, and the dentist guides the patient's decision. The patient interview section begins by noting that oral health, although important, is elective for most people.

nodes.title: PATIENT INTERVIEW
nodes.summary: The text is from Chapter 12 of a prosthodontic textbook, covering diagnosis and treatment planning. It begins with the chapter outline, then discusses the purpose and uniqueness of treatment, emphasizing individualized care based on patient interview and clinical examination. It details the patient interview process, including chief complaint, medical/dental history, expectations, and prior prosthesis experiences. It introduces shared decision making as a model for helping patients choose among treatment options. It states the objectives of prosthodontic treatment: disease elimination, preservation of remaining oral tissues, tooth replacement, and restoration of function and esthetics. The text also notes considerations for treatment planning, including caries, periodontal disease, occlusion, and fixed versus removable replacements. The provided chunk ends as the clinical examination and oral examination sections begin.

nodes.title: CLINICAL EXAMINATION
OBJECTIVES OF PROSTHODONTIC TREATMENT
nodes.summary: The text covers diagnosis and treatment planning in prosthodontics, emphasizing the importance of understanding the patient's chief complaint and history during the interview. It outlines the sequence of patient interview and examination, the role of shared decision making, and the objectives of prosthodontic treatment, including disease elimination, preservation of oral structures, tooth replacement, and functional restoration. It stresses that the removable partial denture treatment plan should be developed before irreversible procedures, using diagnostic casts and thorough evaluation to ensure stability. The text also details the complete oral examination sequence, including prophylaxis, radiographs, vitality tests, temporary restorations, and impressions, as well as the diagnostic value of intraoral radiographs.

nodes.title: ORAL EXAMINATION
nodes.summary: The text covers diagnosis and treatment planning for removable partial dentures, emphasizing that treatment planning must precede irreversible procedures and be guided by diagnostic casts and a master plan. It describes the causes of denture failure, the typical two-appointment complex treatment workflow, and a detailed oral examination sequence including temporary restorations, prophylaxis, radiography, periodontal and ridge evaluation, vitality testing, and floor-of-mouth measurement. It also details the objectives of radiographic examination, factors affecting support and stability, the importance of evaluating occlusion and tissue displaceability, and administrative aspects such as examination fees and record handling. Finally, it explains the construction, materials, and multiple purposes of diagnostic casts, including occlusal analysis, diagnostic waxing, topographic surveying, and patient education.

nodes.title: DIAGNOSTIC CASTS
Purposes of Diagnostic Casts
nodes.summary: The text describes diagnostic procedures and the use of diagnostic casts in removable partial denture treatment planning. It covers clinical examination points such as occlusion problems, vitality testing, floor-of-mouth height determination, and examination fees. It details diagnostic cast requirements, materials, impression techniques, and six main purposes: occlusal analysis, surveying for prosthesis design, patient education, tray fabrication, treatment reference, and permanent records. It also explains articulator selection and mounting, including the axis-orbital plane, arcon/nonarcon articulators, and the facebow mounting sequence.

nodes.title: Mounting Diagnostic Casts
nodes.summary: The text describes using diagnostic casts to plan and communicate removable partial denture framework and mouth modifications, including tooth reshaping guided by the path of placement. It emphasizes keeping unaltered casts as permanent records and using duplicates for alterations. It then discusses mounting diagnostic casts on articulators, explaining when simple hand articulation is sufficient versus when anatomic mounting is needed, and the value of axis-orbital plane orientation. It defines arcon and nonarcon articulators and outlines the initial steps for mounting the maxillary cast using a facebow.

nodes.title: Sequence for Mounting Maxillary Cast to Axis-Orbital Plane
nodes.summary: The text covers diagnosis and treatment planning for removable partial dentures, focusing on the use of diagnostic casts: marking proposed mouth modifications and framework design, duplicating casts for alteration while preserving originals, and mounting casts on an articulator using facebow transfers. It details the axis-orbital plane mounting sequence, facebow types and reference points, arbitrary hinge axis locations, cast preparation, and the Whip-Mix facebow technique. It also addresses jaw relationship records, emphasizing the choice between centric relation and maximum intercuspal position, when to correct occlusal discrepancies, and the recommendation that most removable partial dentures be fabricated in centric relation.

nodes.title: Jaw Relationship Records for Diagnostic Casts
nodes.summary: The text covers facebow transfer procedures and their benefits for accurate articulator mounting, the importance of selecting the correct horizontal jaw relationship (centric relation vs. maximum intercuspal position) for removable partial dentures, and the use of diagnostic casts mounted in centric relation to evaluate and correct occlusal discrepancies. It also describes methods for verifying articulator mountings, adjusting condylar elements with protrusive and lateral records, and the materials and techniques for recording centric relation, including wax, modeling plastic, plaster, metallic oxide paste, and elastomeric materials, along with specific handling and mounting considerations.

nodes.title: Materials and Methods for Recording Centric Relation
nodes.summary: This text covers diagnosis and treatment planning in removable partial dentures, focusing on mounting diagnostic casts on an articulator using facebow transfer and centric relation records, verifying centric relation, and using eccentric records to adjust condylar settings. It describes materials for recording centric relation—wax, modeling plastic, impression plaster, metallic oxide paste, and elastomeric materials—along with their advantages, disadvantages, and recommended uses. The mounting procedure for the mandibular cast with the articulator inverted is detailed. Finally, it discusses diagnostic findings, treatment planning considerations, including financial and medical factors, and notes that removable partial denture treatment generally preserves future treatment options.

This section covers the use of diagnostic casts in removable partial denture treatment planning, including their purposes, requirements, and impression techniques. It details articulator selection and mounting, emphasizing facebow transfers, the axis-orbital plane, and arcon/nonarcon articulators. The maxillary cast mounting sequence is described, including facebow types, arbitrary hinge axis location, and the Whip-Mix technique. Jaw relationship records are addressed, focusing on centric relation versus maximum intercuspal position, verification of mountings, and eccentric records for condylar adjustments. Materials and methods for recording centric relation are explained, along with the mandibular mounting procedure. Finally, diagnostic findings and treatment planning considerations, including financial and medical factors, are discussed, noting that removable partial denture treatment generally preserves future options.

The section covers clinical examination in prosthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning for removable partial dentures. It begins with patient interview, chief complaint, history, shared decision-making, and objectives of prosthodontic treatment: disease elimination, preservation of oral structures, tooth replacement, and functional restoration. It emphasizes establishing the RPD plan before irreversible procedures, using diagnostic casts and a master plan, and details the complete oral examination sequence—prophylaxis, radiographs, vitality tests, temporary restorations, periodontal and ridge evaluation, floor-of-mouth measurement, and impressions—as well as causes of denture failure, support/stability factors, occlusion and tissue displaceability, radiographic objectives, and administrative matters. Diagnostic casts are described regarding construction, materials, requirements, impression techniques, and uses: occlusal analysis, diagnostic waxing, topographic surveying, and patient education. Articulator selection and mounting are covered, including facebow transfers, axis-orbital plane, arcon/nonarcon instruments, maxillary and mandibular mounting sequences, jaw relation records (centric relation versus maximum intercuspal position, eccentric records, materials/methods), and verification. Finally, diagnostic findings and treatment planning considerations, including financial and medical factors and preservation of future options, are discussed.

nodes.title: DIAGNOSTIC FINDINGS
INTERPRETATION OF EXAMINATION DATA
Radiographic and Clinical Evaluation for Partial Dentures
nodes.summary: The page covers preoperative assessment for removable partial dentures, focusing on radiographic interpretation, disease validation, and tooth support. Radiographs help evaluate abutment tooth prognosis, verify caries and periodontal disease severity, and diagnose bone lesions. Clinical examination is essential to confirm radiographic findings. Tooth support emphasizes alveolar bone quality and quantity, the increased loads borne by abutment teeth, management of horizontal forces with rigid connectors, and torque on teeth adjacent to distal extension bases. Proper radiographic interpretation of bone height requires following the lamina dura to the point of decreased opacity, avoiding false bone height caused by angulation. Bone density and past response to loading also aid in predicting prosthesis outcomes.

nodes.title: Index Areas
nodes.summary: The text covers radiographic evaluation of bone quality and its limitations, including normal trabecular and crestal bone appearances, effects of abnormal stresses (bone condensation), and interpretation of radiographic findings as adjuncts to clinical examination. It discusses index areas for assessing alveolar bone reaction to additional stress in abutment teeth, positive and negative bone factors, and the radiographic appearance and significance of the alveolar lamina dura, including changes during tooth tipping and an example involving a mesially tipped lower molar.

nodes.title: Alveolar Lamina Dura
nodes.summary: The text covers diagnostic and treatment planning considerations for prosthetic abutment teeth, focusing on radiographic bone evaluation, index areas, alveolar lamina dura, root morphology, third molars, and periodontal assessment. It emphasizes radiographic limitations, the need for clinical confirmation, bone response to stress, factors influencing abutment prognosis, and the importance of periodontal and oral hygiene evaluation.

nodes.title: Abutment Teeth, Root Morphology, Third Molars, and Periodontal Considerations
nodes.summary: The page covers factors in selecting and evaluating abutment teeth. It explains how bone adapts to tipping forces with lamina dura and trabecular changes, but that systemic health and protein metabolism can affect bone maintenance, so abutment loading must be minimized. Root morphology is important, with multiple divergent roots offering better resistance than fused conical roots. Unerupted third molars can be considered as future abutments to avoid distal extension partial dentures. Periodontal evaluation must assess gingiva, attached mucosa, pockets, bone support, and mobility, and oral hygiene habits must be evaluated and addressed through patient education.

nodes.title: Periodontal Considerations
nodes.summary: The text covers diagnosis and treatment planning for removable partial dentures, including biomechanical effects of tooth tipping and bone adaptation, the influence of root morphology on abutment suitability, and the potential use of unerupted third molars as future abutments. It discusses periodontal evaluation, oral hygiene and maintenance responsibilities, caries risk assessment and preventive measures, xerostomia management, evaluation of the prosthesis foundation on teeth and residual ridges, and surgical preparation such as soft tissue/tori removal, bone augmentation, implants, and indications for tooth extraction.

nodes.title: Caries Risk Assessment and Prosthesis Foundation Evaluation
key_items: Evaluation of the Prosthesis Foundation—Teeth and Residual Ridge
nodes.summary: The page covers long-term oral hygiene and patient responsibility for maintaining removable partial dentures, including regular prophylaxis and maintenance visits. It discusses caries risk assessment, protective restoration choices, sugar intake, fluoride application, xerostomia management, and nutrition referral. It also addresses evaluation of the prosthesis foundation, surgical preparation, removal of interfering tissues or bone, ridge augmentation, implants, and indications for tooth extraction.

nodes.title: Surgical Preparation
nodes.summary: The text covers diagnosis and treatment planning for removable partial dentures, emphasizing long-term oral hygiene and maintenance, caries risk assessment and fluoride/xerostomia management, evaluation of teeth and residual ridge support, pre-prosthetic surgical preparation including extractions and implants, and prosthodontic decision-making based on missing tooth span. It also discusses the need for patient responsibility, plaque control, and endodontic considerations for abutments.

nodes.title: Treatment planning for tooth replacement and removable partial denture abutments
nodes.summary: This page discusses prosthodontic treatment planning for missing teeth, including indications for tooth extraction and comparisons between removable partial dentures, implant-supported prostheses, and fixed prostheses for short modification spaces, longer modification spaces, and distal extension spaces. It also notes endodontic considerations for abutment teeth, particularly distal extension abutments subjected to torsional forces.

nodes.title: Endodontic Treatment
nodes.summary: The text covers diagnosis and treatment planning for removable partial dentures, including indications for tooth extraction, choices among fixed, removable, and implant-supported prostheses for short spans, longer spans, and distal extension spaces, and special considerations for endodontically treated abutments. It also discusses occlusal analysis and adjustment, the selective use of fixed restorations, orthodontic treatment to improve prosthesis design, determination of the mandibular major connector type, and the necessity of properly reshaping remaining teeth before making the master cast.

nodes.title: Removable Partial Denture Planning: Occlusal, Restorative, Orthodontic, and Connector Factors
key_items: Need for Determining Type of Mandibular Major Connector
nodes.summary: This page covers key factors in removable partial denture planning: evaluating endodontically treated abutments and overdenture abutments for distal extension control; analyzing occlusal factors to accept or improve existing occlusion before prosthesis fabrication; deciding when fixed restorations are preferable to RPDs for modification spaces and tooth-bounded areas; using orthodontic treatment to improve RPD design; determining the mandibular major connector type during oral examination by measuring the floor-of-mouth height; and reshaping remaining teeth to provide guiding planes, rest areas, and favorable contours for successful prosthesis support.

nodes.title: Need for Reshaping Remaining Teeth
nodes.summary: The passage discusses treatment planning for partially edentulous patients, including risks with endodontically treated distal-extension abutments, occlusal analysis and harmonization before prosthesis fabrication, indications for fixed restorations, orthodontic treatment and implant-assisted anchorage, selection of the mandibular major connector, necessary reshaping of teeth for guiding planes and clasps, CDC-based infection control protocols and disinfection/sterilization measures, and the initial consideration of fixed versus removable partial dentures in total oral rehabilitation.

The section covers interpretation of examination data for removable partial denture treatment planning. It emphasizes integrating medical history, prior prosthesis experience, and clinical/radiographic findings. A framework combines disease management (radiographic, periodontal, caries, endodontic) with reconstruction considerations (prosthesis support from teeth and ridges, and design-specific factors). Abutment evaluation includes bone density, lamina dura, index areas, root morphology, third molars, and torque on distal-extension abutments. Periodontal, caries-risk, hygiene, and maintenance factors are addressed. Foundation evaluation and surgical preparation include extractions, tori removal, augmentation, and implants. Tooth replacement options compare fixed, removable, and implant-supported prostheses for different spaces. Additional planning aspects include endodontic treatment, occlusal analysis, fixed restorations, orthodontics, mandibular connector selection, reshaping teeth, and infection control.

nodes.title: INFECTION CONTROL
nodes.summary: The text covers prosthodontic assessment, noting that tooth inclination relative to the path of placement and retentive/supportive areas cannot be judged visually and requires surveyor analysis of diagnostic casts. It then discusses infection control in dentistry per CDC/ADA recommendations, including the 2003 updates, standard precautions, potential pathogens, transmission routes, chain of infection, laundry measures, referral of infectious patients, and disinfection/sterilization protocols for instruments and laboratory materials. Finally, it begins a section on differential diagnosis of fixed versus removable partial dentures, emphasizing total oral rehabilitation for partially edentulous patients.

nodes.title: DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: FIXED OR REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES
Tooth-Bounded Edentulous Regions and Modification Spaces in Partial Denture Planning
nodes.summary: This page from Chapter 12 covers treatment planning for partially edentulous arches, focusing on tooth-bounded edentulous regions and modification spaces. It states that fixed partial dentures are generally preferred for bounded edentulous spans when abutments are suitable, with the number of abutments determined by span length and periodontal support; implants are an alternative. It discusses management of nonparallel abutments, conservative retainers, and contraindications to unilateral fixed restorations. Unilateral removable partial dentures are strongly discouraged. Modification spaces, especially opposite-side spaces in Class III arches, can improve removable partial denture support and simplify design, but lone-standing abutments may require fixed restoration or splinting. Anterior missing teeth are usually fixed replacements, with exceptions for esthetic benefits or simplified treatment by inclusion in a removable partial denture.

nodes.title: Anterior Modification Spaces
nodes.summary: The text discusses treatment planning for partially edentulous arches, focusing on when to choose fixed versus removable partial dentures. It covers Class III modification spaces, the discouraged use of unilateral removable partial dentures, indications for fixed restorations in tooth-bounded edentulous regions, contraindications to unilateral fixed restorations, management of modification spaces, anterior modification spaces, and replacement of unilaterally missing molars. Key principles include cross-arch stabilization, abutment selection, conservative retainers, implant alternatives, splinting lone abutments, esthetic considerations, and the use of cantilever or distal extension prostheses for missing molars.

nodes.title: Replacement of Unilaterally Missing Molars (Shortened Dental Arch)
nodes.summary: The text discusses treatment planning for partially edentulous patients, focusing on anterior tooth replacement, unilaterally missing molars, and indications for removable partial dentures. It emphasizes that anterior replacements are usually best with fixed prostheses unless ridge defects or resorption make removable options more favorable. For unilaterally missing molars, decisions must balance treatment impact and long-term benefit; options include cantilever fixed prostheses, implants, or removable distal extension prostheses, with considerations for opposing teeth and maxillary tuberosity. Removable partial dentures are specifically indicated for distal extension situations, after recent extractions, and for long spans, with attention to Kennedy Class I/II cases, temporary resin dentures, relining needs, and adequate support.

nodes.title: Removable Partial Dentures: Indications, Distal Extension, Extractions, Long Span
nodes.summary: The page covers indications for removable partial dentures, focusing on distal extension situations, recent extractions, and long spans. It explains that RPDs are used when fixed restorations are contraindicated, and that unilateral distal extension decisions depend on opposing teeth and the maxillary tuberosity. RPDs are commonly indicated for Kennedy Class I and II cases when implants are not feasible, except when certain molar replacements are unnecessary or can be managed with fixed cantilevers or implants. After recent extractions, temporary or resin RPDs are recommended because they are inexpensive, relinable, and adaptable before future restorations. Long-span prostheses can be tooth-supported with adequate abutments and framework rigidity.

nodes.title: Long Span
nodes.summary: The text discusses diagnosis and treatment planning for removable partial dentures (RPDs), emphasizing specific indications and clinical considerations. It covers unilateral distal extension cases, where opposing teeth and maxillary tuberosity effects are important, and outlines indications for RPDs: distal extension situations, recent extractions, long spans, need for bilateral stabilization in periodontal disease, and excessive residual bone loss. In these contexts, RPDs offer advantages over fixed restorations by providing cross-arch stabilization, allowing future modifications, better accommodating tissue changes, and enabling more natural tooth positioning despite ridge resorption.

nodes.title: Bilateral Stabilization and Residual Bone Loss in Prosthodontics
key_items: Need for Effect of Bilateral Stabilization
nodes.summary: The page compares fixed and removable partial dentures, emphasizing the need for bilateral stabilization and management of excessive residual bone loss. It states that removable partial dentures provide similar abutment support to fixed restorations but avoid excessive torque through cross-arch stabilization, and can serve as periodontal splints in periodontally weakened mouths. With excessive ridge resorption, fixed pontics often occupy poor positions, especially anteriorly, leading to unnatural tooth placement, poor lip support, and esthetic problems; removable partial dentures with labial flanges allow more natural positioning. Mandibular anterior fixed bridges may require tooth omission or narrowing and follow the resorbed ridge, whereas removable partial dentures permit favorable placement relative to the lip and opposing teeth, provided positive abutment support is obtained. The accompanying figure shows a Kennedy Class IV ridge defect and vertical bone loss favoring a removable partial denture.

nodes.title: Removable Partial Denture Abutment and Treatment Planning Considerations
nodes.summary: The page discusses removable partial denture treatment planning for abutment teeth. It explains that even unusually sound teeth should be modified with guiding planes, occlusal rests, and stabilizing surfaces to provide proper prosthesis support and durability. For abutments with guarded prognoses, the denture can be designed to allow future modification or addition of teeth, with special considerations for posterior versus anterior abutments and provisions for indirect retention, clasping, and tissue support. Economic factors should not be the sole deciding criterion; compromise treatment must be clearly presented as such, as it may offer limited success and prove more costly over time. A figure demonstrates a Kennedy Class II modification 1 case with a questionable molar abutment and clasp designs intended to accommodate potential future distal extension.

The opening text covers visual examination followed by surveyor analysis and reviews CDC infection-control recommendations for dental practice, including standard precautions, transmission routes, instrument/laboratory disinfection, and decontamination communication. The main section compares fixed and removable partial dentures in the total rehabilitation of partially edentulous patients. Fixed prostheses are generally preferred for bounded edentulous spans and anterior teeth when abutments are suitable, with implants as an alternative; unilateral removable partial dentures are discouraged. Removable partial dentures are indicated for distal extension situations, recent extractions, long spans, periodontal bilateral stabilization, and excessive ridge resorption, offering cross-arch stabilization and favorable esthetics. The section also addresses modification spaces, missing molar options, abutment preparation, design flexibility, and the role of economic considerations in treatment planning.

nodes.title: CHOICE BETWEEN COMPLETE DENTURES AND REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES
nodes.summary: The text covers two main topics: choosing between complete dentures and removable partial dentures for partially edentulous patients, and clinical factors related to metal alloys used for RPD frameworks. The decision-making section addresses tooth prognosis, functional expectations, patient preferences, tooth location and distribution, risks of retaining only anterior teeth, and interim prostheses. The alloy section discusses advantages of cast frameworks, common chromium-cobalt alloy composition and properties, titanium limitations, comparisons between gold and Cr-Co alloys, and their relative physical properties such as yield strength.

nodes.title: CLINICAL FACTORS RELATED TO METAL ALLOYS USED FOR REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURE FRAMEWORKS
key_items: Comparative Physical Properties of Gold and Chromium-Cobalt
Wrought Wire: Selection and Quality Control
nodes.summary: The text covers removable partial denture treatment planning considerations, including respecting patient wishes, interim dentures, and the pros and cons of retaining only mandibular anterior teeth. It then discusses metal frameworks for RPDs, emphasizing the advantages of cast Cr-Co alloys over acrylic, their composition, and a detailed comparison of physical properties with gold alloys, including flexibility, yield strength, stiffness, weight, hardness, and clinical implications. Titanium and titanium alloys are reviewed as potential future materials, with current fabrication limitations. Finally, the selection and quality control of wrought-wire retainer arms are described, including attachment methods, important physical properties, ADA specifications, and the recommendation to taper wires to 0.8 mm for better stress distribution.

nodes.title: SUMMARY
nodes.summary: The text first emphasizes that dental fundamentals are inviolable; only methods, procedures, and substances change, and the dentist must evaluate all factors and make decisions that best serve the patient. It then introduces the chapter on preparation of the mouth for removable partial dentures, outlining four categories: oral surgical preparation, conditioning of abused and irritated tissues, periodontal preparation, and abutment teeth preparation. Mouth preparation is described as fundamental, following preliminary diagnosis and tentative treatment planning, with the goal of restoring oral health and removing conditions detrimental to the prosthesis. It must be completed before master impressions, and surgical/periodontal procedures should precede abutment preparation with adequate healing time, ideally at least 6 weeks to 3-6 months. The chapter outline lists specific procedures under each category, including surgical extractions and soft tissue lesions, tissue conditioning materials, phases of periodontal therapy, and abutment restorations, wax patterns, and rest seats.

The section covers diagnostic findings and treatment planning for removable partial dentures. It begins with articulator mounting using verified wax or elastomeric interocclusal records and then explains how interview and examination data guide treatment decisions. It covers interpretation of examination data, including abutment evaluation, disease management, surgical/prosthodontic preparation, and tooth replacement options. Infection control protocols per CDC/ADA are reviewed. Differential diagnosis is provided for fixed versus removable partial dentures, including implant and complete denture considerations. The section also discusses metal framework alloys, especially Cr-Co and titanium, and wrought-wire retainers. Finally, it outlines the four categories of mouth preparation and emphasizes healing times before definitive prosthetic procedures.

structure.summary: This section covers diagnosis and treatment planning for removable partial dentures. It starts with the chapter's topics and the four-step treatment planning process: interview, examination, individualized plan, and sequenced treatment with follow-up. The patient interview includes chief complaint, medical/dental history, expectations, prior prosthesis experience, and shared decision making. Prosthodontic objectives are disease elimination, preservation of remaining oral tissues, tooth replacement, and restoration of function and esthetics. Clinical examination emphasizes establishing the RPD plan before irreversible procedures, using diagnostic casts and a master plan, and includes a complete oral examination sequence, factors affecting denture support/stability, occlusion, radiographic objectives, and administrative matters. Diagnostic casts are described for occlusal analysis, diagnostic waxing, surveying, and patient education. Articulator selection and mounting, facebow transfers, and jaw relation records are covered. Diagnosis and treatment planning include interpretation of examination data, abutment evaluation, infection control per CDC/ADA, differential diagnosis of fixed vs removable vs implant vs complete dentures, metal alloys (Cr-Co, titanium, wrought-wire retainers), four categories of mouth preparation, healing times, financial/medical considerations, and preservation of future options.

nodes.title: ORAL SURGICAL PREPARATION
Preprosthetic Oral Surgery for Removable Partial Dentures
nodes.summary: The page covers preprosthetic oral surgery in removable partial denture treatment. It emphasizes coordinating extractions and other surgical procedures with the overall treatment plan, allowing healing time before impressions, and assigning the dentist responsibility for surgical follow-through. It describes indications for extracting nonstrategic or doubtful teeth, removing retained root tips/fragments, and removing impacted teeth to prevent periodontal complications and improve denture stability. It also notes anxiety-control measures and uses figures to show diagnostic evaluation and root-tip removal.

nodes.title: Impacted Teeth
nodes.summary: The text discusses mouth preparation for removable partial dentures, emphasizing coordinated surgical planning, the dentist's responsibility for surgical care, and management of specific oral conditions. It covers planned extractions based on strategic tooth evaluation, removal of residual roots and impacted teeth with appropriate monitoring in elderly patients, correction of malposed teeth via orthodontics or surgical repositioning, and the need for panoramic imaging to detect cysts and tumors.

nodes.title: Malposed Teeth
nodes.summary: The text discusses preparation of the mouth for removable partial dentures, focusing on management of impacted teeth, malposed teeth, and cysts/odontogenic tumors. It advises leaving asymptomatic impacted teeth in elderly patients when covered by bone and without pathology, but emphasizes documenting them, informing the patient, and monitoring with radiographs. Because jaw changes may expose impacted teeth via sinus tracts and cause serious infections, early removal is recommended, and any impacted tooth reachable by a periodontal probe must be extracted. Tooth loss can cause extrusion or drifting of remaining teeth; while orthodontics may help, surgical repositioning of teeth and alveolar bone is an outpatient alternative that should be considered before compromising denture design. Panoramic radiographs are recommended to detect unsuspected cysts and tumors.

nodes.title: Cysts and Odontogenic Tumors
nodes.summary: The text covers preparation of the mouth for removable partial dentures, including management of impacted teeth in the elderly, correction of malposed teeth, evaluation of cysts and odontogenic tumors, removal of exostoses and tori, excision of hyperplastic tissue, and management of problematic muscle attachments and frena. It emphasizes preserving bone and arch morphology, avoiding compromised denture designs, confirming pathologic diagnoses through biopsy/pathology, and using surgical stents for healing.

nodes.title: Oral Abnormalities: Exostoses, Hyperplastic Tissue, and Muscle Attachments
nodes.summary: The page covers the evaluation of suspicious jaw lesions through periapical radiographs, consultation, and biopsy; the management of exostoses and tori to avoid denture complications and periodontal damage; the removal of hyperplastic tissue to create a stable denture foundation and improve prosthetic outcomes; and the beginning of a discussion on muscle attachments and frena in relation to residual ridge bone loss.

nodes.title: Muscle Attachments and Frena
nodes.summary: The text covers mouth preparation for removable partial dentures: investigating suspicious radiographic and soft-tissue lesions with biopsy/pathology; removing or managing exostoses/tori and hyperplastic tissue; repositioning problematic muscle attachments and frena; correcting bony spines and knife-edge ridges; excising polyps, papillomas, hemangiomas, hyperkeratoses, erythroplasia, and ulcerations before prosthesis fabrication; evaluating and treating dentofacial deformities with a multidisciplinary approach; using osseointegrated implants, particularly Brånemark titanium implants, to enhance prosthesis support; and considering alveolar ridge augmentation with autogenous or alloplastic materials.

nodes.title: Preparing the Mouth for Removable Partial Dentures
nodes.summary: The page covers surgical preparation of the mouth before removable partial denture fabrication. It describes managing bony spines, knife-edge ridges, muscle attachments, frena, and grafts; excising and biopsying abnormal soft-tissue and mucosal lesions; multidisciplinary evaluation and treatment planning for dentofacial deformities; use of osseointegrated implants to improve prosthesis stability; and ridge augmentation with autogenous or alloplastic materials.

nodes.title: Augmentation of Alveolar Bone
nodes.summary: The text describes surgical and preparatory procedures for the mouth before fabricating removable partial dentures. It covers management of bony protuberances, muscle attachments, frena, bony spines, and knife-edge ridges; excision and biopsy of abnormal soft tissue and mucosal lesions; evaluation and surgical planning for dentofacial deformities; use of osseointegrated implants, especially Brånemark-type implants; alveolar ridge augmentation options and limitations; and conditioning of abused/irritated tissues before final impressions.

This section covers preprosthetic oral surgical preparation for removable partial dentures. It emphasizes completing surgery early, coordinating it with the treatment plan, allowing adequate healing time, and assigning the dentist responsibility for surgical follow-through. It details management of extractions, residual roots, impacted teeth, malposed teeth, cysts and odontogenic tumors, exostoses and tori, hyperplastic tissue, muscle attachments and frena, bony spines and knife-edge ridges, soft-tissue lesions, dentofacial deformities, osseointegrated implants, and alveolar ridge augmentation. The overall goal is to return the mouth to optimum health and eliminate conditions that could compromise the prosthesis.

nodes.title: CONDITIONING OF ABUSED AND IRRITATED TISSUES
nodes.summary: This text covers preparation of the mouth for removable partial dentures, including examples of implant-supported and retained prostheses, and emphasizes proper implant placement, support, and protection from occlusal forces. It then focuses on conditioning abused and irritated oral tissues before final impressions, describing symptoms, causes, and the need to rule out systemic conditions. It outlines a home care program and the use of tissue conditioning materials, including specific steps for achieving maximum benefit, the importance of extending and relieving denture bases, and the expected treatment schedule and need for medical referral if no improvement occurs.

nodes.title: PERIODONTAL PREPARATION*
Periodontal Preparation, Objectives, Diagnosis and Treatment Planning
nodes.summary: The page covers periodontal preparation in relation to removable partial denture treatment, emphasizing that periodontal therapy must be completed before restorative procedures. It outlines the objectives and criteria for successful periodontal therapy, the need for complete periodontal charting, and the systematic diagnosis of periodontal disease through probing, bleeding assessment, radiographs, and mobility grading. It also stresses that periodontal health must be established before fabricating a removable partial denture.

nodes.title: Diagnosis
nodes.summary: The text discusses periodontal preparation for removable partial dentures, emphasizing that periodontal health must be established before restorative treatment. It covers the relationship between periodontal therapy and oral surgery, the objectives and criteria for successful periodontal therapy, comprehensive periodontal diagnosis including probing, radiography, and mobility grading, and the three-phase periodontal treatment plan. It also details phase 1 disease control: oral hygiene instruction, scaling and root planing, and correction of local irritants, all aimed at ensuring the supporting structures are healthy before prosthesis fabrication.

nodes.title: Mouth Preparation for Removable Partial Dentures
nodes.summary: The text describes periodontal preparation of the mouth before fabricating removable partial dentures. It covers assessment of tooth mobility, a three-phase periodontal treatment plan, initial disease control therapy including oral hygiene instruction and scaling/root planing, and correction of local irritating factors such as overhanging margins and open contacts.

nodes.title: Elimination of Local Irritating Factors Other Than Calculus
nodes.summary: This text covers preparation of the mouth for removable partial dentures, focusing on periodontal evaluation and treatment. Tooth mobility is assessed to determine whether teeth can support a prosthesis. Periodontal care is organized into three phases: initial disease control, surgical treatment, and maintenance. Phase 1 includes oral hygiene instruction, scaling and root planing, removal of local irritants, and occlusal adjustment. Oral hygiene instruction emphasizes patient education and demonstrated plaque control before definitive treatment. Scaling and root planing using ultrasonic instruments and curettes is fundamental. Overhanging restorations and open contacts should be corrected, and urgent caries may be treated early. Occlusal interferences are managed by selective grinding only when pathologic. A detailed guide by Schuyler is provided for occlusal adjustment by selective grinding, covering centric relation contacts, eccentric interferences, balancing-side contacts, and preservation of static centric support. The overall goal is a stable, healthy periodontium capable of supporting a removable partial denture.

nodes.title: Elimination of Gross Occlusal Interferences
nodes.summary: The text covers occlusal and periodontal treatment. It emphasizes early management of severe caries with pulpal involvement, then discusses elimination of gross occlusal interferences by selective grinding. Plaque and calculus are primary periodontal disease factors, but poor restorations and occlusal interferences can accelerate attachment loss. Selective grinding is used to remove traumatic and deflective contacts, establish centric relation, and eliminate working/nonworking interferences; adjustment is indicated only when pathology exists, and bilateral balanced occlusion is unnecessary in natural dentition. The text then presents Schuyler's guide to occlusal adjustment: use mounted diagnostic casts, first achieve static maximum intercuspal contact in centric relation using specific grinding rules, then evaluate and correct eccentric and balancing contacts while preserving static centric support.

nodes.title: Guide to Occlusal Adjustment
nodes.summary: The text covers mouth preparation for removable partial dentures, including early management of carious lesions, elimination of occlusal interferences via selective grinding, guidelines for occlusal adjustment, temporary and permanent splinting of mobile teeth, and use of a nightguard. It emphasizes treating caries early, adjusting occlusion only when pathology exists while preserving centric contacts, using specific grinding rules for centric, balancing, working, and protrusive relations, managing tooth mobility through appropriate splinting techniques, and using a flat acrylic-resin nightguard to reduce lateral forces, especially when the denture is removed or an unopposed abutment is returned to function.

nodes.title: Temporary Splinting
nodes.summary: The text covers occlusal correction principles for removable partial dentures, temporary splinting of mobile teeth, and use of a nightguard. It details which cusps should be preserved and which surfaces ground to relieve working-side, balancing-side, and protrusive prematurities while maintaining centric contacts. It discusses evaluating mobile teeth, reversible vs irreversible mobility, methods of temporary immobilization, and options for permanent splinting, including cast restorations and RPD design. It also describes the nightguard as a temporary stabilization device worn when the RPD is removed, its flat occlusal design to reduce lateral forces, and its value when an unopposed abutment tooth is being returned to function.

nodes.title: Use of a Nightguard
nodes.summary: The text discusses preparation of the mouth for removable partial dentures, covering selective grinding principles for occlusal corrections, temporary and permanent splinting of mobile teeth, use of a nightguard for unopposed teeth and clenching, minor tooth movement for better RPD support, and definitive periodontal surgery including periodontal flaps, guided tissue regeneration, and periodontal plastic surgery.

nodes.title: Minor Tooth Movement
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal considerations in restorative dentistry, including the role of nightguards in reversing ligament changes, adjunctive minor tooth movement for better prosthetic outcomes, and definitive Phase 2 periodontal surgery.
