It describes periodontal flaps and their goals, osseous resection techniques, guided tissue regeneration (GTR) with membranes and grafts, and periodontal plastic surgery with its objectives and common procedures.

nodes.title: Periodontal Surgery
nodes.summary: The text discusses preparation of the mouth for removable partial dentures. It covers reversal of periodontal ligament changes with a nightguard, minor tooth movement to improve abutment stability, and definitive periodontal surgery (Phase 2), including periodontal flaps, osseous resection, guided tissue regeneration, and periodontal plastic surgery. It also describes Phase 3 recall maintenance and the advantages of periodontal therapy before prosthesis fabrication, such as preventing tooth loss, improving the restorative environment, reevaluating questionable teeth, and assessing patient cooperation. Finally, it begins abutment teeth preparation, emphasizing the use of diagnostic casts, survey, path of placement, rest seats, guiding planes, and abutment restorations.

nodes.title: Periodontal Therapy, Maintenance, and Abutment Preparation
nodes.summary: The page covers a gingival recession case treated with a subepithelial connective tissue graft, the importance of Phase 3 recall maintenance after periodontal therapy, the advantages of periodontal therapy before removable partial dentures, and the initial steps of abutment teeth preparation using diagnostic casts and survey information.

The section covers periodontal preparation for removable partial dentures, emphasizing that periodontal health must be established before restorative procedures. It describes comprehensive periodontal diagnosis, a three-phase treatment plan, and Phase 1 disease control including oral hygiene instruction, scaling and root planing, removal of local irritants, caries management, and selective occlusal grinding using Schuyler's guidelines. It also covers temporary and permanent splinting, nightguard use, minor tooth movement, definitive Phase 2 periodontal surgery (flaps, osseous resection, guided tissue regeneration, and plastic surgery), Phase 3 maintenance, the advantages of completing periodontal therapy before prosthesis fabrication, and initial abutment preparation using diagnostic casts and survey information.

nodes.title: ABUTMENT TEETH PREPARATION
nodes.summary: The text covers periodontal and prosthodontic preparation for removable partial dentures (RPDs). It describes treating gingival recession with subepithelial connective tissue grafts, maintaining periodontal health through customized recall, and the advantages of periodontal therapy before RPD fabrication. It then details abutment tooth preparation, including evaluation with diagnostic casts, restoration selection, guiding-plane preparation, surveyed crowns, wax-pattern contouring, and proper occlusal rest seat form. Emphasis is placed on avoiding caries at proximal gingival areas, directing forces axially through properly shaped rests, and the importance of thorough mouth preparation for RPD success. The passage closes by introducing Chapter 14, which outlines and discusses abutment preparation after surgical/periodontal/endodontic treatment, management of lost or questionable abutments, and considerations for RPD design and future modifications.

structure.summary: This section covers comprehensive preparation of the mouth for removable partial dentures, including oral surgical preparation, conditioning of abused and irritated tissues, periodontal preparation, and abutment teeth preparation. It stresses early, coordinated surgery with adequate healing; resolving irritations before final impressions; establishing periodontal health through phased treatment; and properly preparing abutment teeth with accurate restorations, guiding planes, surveyed crowns, and rest seats. The overall goal is a healthy oral environment that supports successful RPD fabrication and function.

structure.title: Preparation of Abutment Teeth

nodes.title: Abutment tooth classification and preparation sequences for removable partial dentures
key_items: SEQUENCE OF ABUTMENT PREPARATIONS ON SOUND ENAMEL OR EXISTING RESTORATIONS
nodes.summary: The page covers classification of abutment teeth for removable partial dentures, including the three types of abutment preparation and the considerations for unprotected abutments, complete coverage versus amalgam restorations, and newer composite options. It then details the recommended sequence for preparing abutments on sound enamel or acceptable existing restorations, from guiding planes and contour modification to verification with a surveyor and occlusal rest preparation. Finally, it discusses conservative abutment preparations using inlays, emphasizing margin extension beyond line angles to withstand clasp contact and maintain a strong restoration-tooth junction.

nodes.title: ABUTMENT PREPARATIONS USING CONSERVATIVE RESTORATIONS
nodes.summary: The text covers classification of abutment teeth for removable partial dentures, grouping them into minor coronal modifications, conservative restorations, and complete coverage crowns. It describes the sequence of mouth preparation on sound enamel or acceptable restorations: proximal guiding planes, contour reduction for clasp placement, surveyor verification via a cast, and occlusal rest seats. It also discusses conservative inlay preparations, including outline modifications, pulp protection, resistance/retention requirements, and the special issue of mandibular premolars. For crown abutments, it emphasizes making multiple wax patterns on a surveyor, paralleling guiding planes, carving rest seats, preserving critical areas during spruing/polishing, and using complete coverage, porcelain veneer, or three-quarter crowns appropriately. Figures illustrate the sequence and clinical examples.

nodes.title: ABUTMENT PREPARATIONS USING CROWNS
Ledges on Abutment Crowns
nodes.summary: This section discusses preparing abutment teeth for removable partial dentures, emphasizing the importance of planning occlusal rest spaces and creating crown ledges. It explains how crown ledges enable true reciprocation, stabilization, and indirect retention by providing a parallel guiding surface for the reciprocal clasp arm. The text covers ledge design, placement, wax pattern carving, post-casting refinement using surveyors or milling machines, proper polishing, and spark erosion technology to achieve precise fit while maintaining cast orientation.

nodes.title: Spark Erosion
nodes.summary: The text discusses achieving precision in abutment tooth preparations for removable partial dentures, emphasizing that crown ledges and proximal guiding planes must be refined after casting to remain parallel to the path of placement. This is accomplished using surveyor-mounted handpiece holders, specific burs and stones, or milling machines. The reciprocal clasp arm is waxed onto the casting, and careful polishing is needed to preserve prepared surfaces. Spark erosion is described as an advanced technique for precision fit, and maintaining the original cast orientation is critical throughout. The accompanying figure illustrates a milling machine used to prepare parallel surfaces and rest seats while preserving the established path of placement.

nodes.title: Veneer Crowns for Support of Clasp Arms
nodes.summary: The text covers two main topics: veneer crowns used on abutment teeth for clasp support, and splinting of abutment teeth. It describes types of veneer crowns, the importance of proper contouring to achieve retention, survey before cementation, and material considerations—noting that glazed porcelain resists wear better than resin and that resin veneers should be used with metal support. It also explains when and how to splint weak abutment teeth, common combinations like premolars and canines, the need to avoid retaining periodontally hopeless teeth, and methods such as casting/soldering crowns together with possible splint bars for stabilization.

The section covers preparing abutment crowns for removable partial dentures, emphasizing surveyor-controlled fabrication of multiple wax patterns to achieve parallel guiding planes, proper occlusal rest seats, and controlled contours. It discusses ideal crown types—complete coverage, porcelain veneer, and three-quarter crowns—and their advantages and limitations. Subtopics detail crown ledges for reciprocal clasp arms, post-casting refinement using milling machines and spark erosion, veneer crown contouring and material considerations, and splinting of weak abutment teeth. Throughout, preserving the established path of placement and avoiding damage to critical prepared surfaces are stressed.

nodes.title: SPLINTING OF ABUTMENT TEETH
nodes.summary: The text discusses veneer crowns used to support clasp arms on removable partial denture abutments, emphasizing cosmetic metal avoidance, types of veneers, contouring for retention, and wear considerations of porcelain versus resin. It then covers splinting of weak abutment teeth, including indications, common premolar and canine splinting, management of lingual rests on anterior teeth, and rare molar splinting such as hemisected roots. Finally, it addresses isolated teeth as abutments, their unfavorable forces, the use of additional abutments for stabilization, and the recommendation to splint an isolated anterior abutment adjacent to a distal extension base to the nearest tooth with a fixed partial denture.

nodes.title: USE OF ISOLATED TEETH AS ABUTMENTS
nodes.summary: The text covers preparation of abutment teeth for removable partial dentures, focusing on splinting principles. It discusses use of mandibular anterior teeth, lingual rest placement and load distribution, molar splinting exceptions, and management of isolated abutment teeth through additional abutments or fixed partial denture splinting. It also addresses replacement of missing anterior teeth, emphasizing fixed restorations over including anterior segments in removable partial dentures, with consideration of biomechanical support, esthetics, economics, and the need for patient responsibility when compromises are made.

nodes.title: MISSING ANTERIOR TEETH
nodes.summary: The text covers two main prosthodontic topics. First, it discusses the management of isolated tooth abutments and missing anterior teeth in removable partial denture treatment. It emphasizes splinting isolated terminal abutments with fixed partial dentures to provide multiple abutment support, and generally recommends replacing missing anterior teeth with fixed restorations rather than including them in an RPD, except when ridge resorption or esthetics requires a denture base; splint bars and multiple rest seats can improve support. Second, it describes a technique for making temporary acrylic-resin crowns while an existing removable partial denture remains in use, including impression-making with the denture in place, resin injection, reseating the denture to maintain occlusion, and finishing the crowns.

nodes.title: TEMPORARY CROWNS WHEN A REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURE IS BEING WORN
nodes.summary: The text covers principles and procedures for preparing abutment teeth for removable partial dentures. It describes optimizing anterior tooth support with multiple prepared rest seats, managing anterior ridge resorption, and using splint bars and dual-path placement. It details making temporary crowns while an existing RPD remains in use, including impression with the RPD in place, resin injection technique, finishing, and cementation. It also explains the indirect-direct technique for fabricating a crown that fits an existing RPD clasp: temporary crown, resin coping on a stone die, functional wax-up of occlusion, proximal contacts, and clasp contacts, followed by final pattern adjustments.

nodes.title: FABRICATING RESTORATIONS TO FIT EXISTING DENTURE RETAINERS
nodes.summary: The text covers clinical procedures for temporary crown cementation and for fabricating crowns to fit existing removable partial denture retainers, including detailed steps for impressions, resin copings, wax patterns, clasp adaptation, and creation of retention. It also introduces impression materials for removable partial dentures, classifying them as rigid, thermoplastic, or elastic, explains why elastic materials are generally used, and begins discussion of plaster of Paris as a rigid impression material.

structure.summary: The section covers preparation of abutment teeth for removable partial dentures, beginning with treatment timing, prognosis, and management of questionable abutments. It describes classification of abutment preparations and the sequence for preparing sound enamel or existing restorations, including guiding planes, contour modification, surveyor verification, and occlusal rest seats. Conservative restorations such as inlays and newer composite options are discussed, along with crown abutment preparations using complete coverage, porcelain veneer, and three-quarter crowns, emphasizing surveyor-controlled waxing, parallel guiding planes, ledges, and post-casting refinement including spark erosion. The text also addresses veneer crowns for clasp support, splinting of weak abutments, isolated teeth as abutments, and management of missing anterior teeth. Techniques are provided for making temporary crowns while an existing RPD is worn, fabricating crowns to fit existing denture retainers, and using appropriate impression materials for RPDs.

structure.title: Impression Materials and Procedures for Removable Partial Dentures

nodes.title: RIGID MATERIALS*
nodes.summary: The text covers the classification and use of impression materials for removable partial dentures, focusing on rigid materials (plaster of Paris and metallic oxide paste) and thermoplastic materials (modeling plastic). It explains the properties, indications, handling, and precautions for each material, emphasizing that elastic materials are generally preferred for accurate impressions involving undercuts. It also includes details on border molding, custom trays, and the limitations of rigid and thermoplastic materials. The chapter outline additionally mentions procedures for hydrocolloid impressions and individual acrylic-resin trays, though the given text mainly elaborates on rigid and thermoplastic materials.

nodes.title: THERMOPLASTIC MATERIALS*
nodes.summary: The text discusses impression materials and procedures for removable partial dentures, covering rigid materials (plaster of Paris and metallic oxide paste), thermoplastic materials (modeling plastic and mouth-temperature impression waxes/resins), and elastic materials (reversible and irreversible hydrocolloids, and mercaptan rubber-base). It details their composition, uses, handling, advantages, limitations, and clinical precautions, including specific notes on border molding, tray requirements, storage, disinfection, and relining applications.

nodes.title: ELASTIC MATERIALS*
key_items: Polyether Impression Materials; Silicone Impression Materials
nodes.summary: The text covers impression materials and procedures for removable partial dentures. It describes modeling plastic sticks for border molding, mouth-temperature impression waxes and natural resins, including their flow, correction, relining, and storage characteristics. It then reviews elastic materials: reversible and irreversible hydrocolloids, mercaptan rubber-base, polyether, and silicone impression materials, highlighting their accuracy, working times, dimensional stability, tissue detail, disinfection, and clinical limitations. Finally, it addresses impressions of the partially edentulous arch, emphasizing the need to accurately record tooth and tissue anatomy for proper fit and retention and to avoid materials that permanently deform when removed from undercuts.

nodes.title: IMPRESSIONS OF THE PARTIALLY EDENTULOUS ARCH
Step-by-Step Procedure for Making a Stone Cast From a Hydrocolloid Impression
nodes.summary: The text details the step-by-step procedure for making a stone cast from a hydrocolloid impression, emphasizing correct material selection, mixing, vibration, incremental pouring to avoid air entrapment, proper base thickness, moisture control, and timely separation. It then lists possible causes of inaccurate or weak casts, including impression distortion, incorrect water-powder ratio, improper mixing, trapped air, hydrocolloid-related chalky surfaces, and premature or delayed separation. Finally, it discusses the need for individual impression trays when stock trays are unsuitable, and describes the technique for fabricating custom acrylic-resin trays, including the use of duplicate diagnostic casts and visible light-cured materials.

nodes.title: Possible Causes of an Inaccurate and/or a Weak Cast of a Dental Arch
nodes.summary: The text describes dental cast trimming and finishing procedures, then lists causes of inaccurate or weak dental arch casts, including hydrocolloid distortion, incorrect water-powder ratio, improper mixing, trapped air, surface defects, and improper separation timing. It then discusses when individual impression trays are necessary, the limitations of stock trays, and advantages of custom acrylic-resin trays for accurate border impressions. It also covers final impression material choices and the technique for fabricating individual acrylic-resin trays, including the use of visible light-cured tray materials.

The section covers principles and procedures for making impressions of the partially edentulous arch. It begins with detailed evaluations of elastic impression materials—mercaptan rubber base, polyether, and silicone—highlighting accuracy, handling, working times, sterilization, and limitations. It then explains the need for impressions to accurately record teeth and tissues without permanent deformation, excluding thermoplastic materials and metallic oxide pastes and cautioning against highly cross-linked rubber-base materials in large undercuts. Hydrocolloid materials are extensively described: reversible versus irreversible forms, their advantages for undercuts, dimensional instability, syneresis, necessary precautions, and a step-by-step clinical procedure for making a hydrocolloid impression. Finally, the section covers making a stone cast from a hydrocolloid impression, possible causes of inaccurate or weak casts, and the indications and fabrication of custom acrylic-resin impression trays, including visible light-cured tray materials.

nodes.title: INDIVIDUAL IMPRESSION TRAYS
key_items: Technique for Making Individual Acrylic-Resin Impression Trays
nodes.summary: The text covers dental cast and impression procedures for removable partial dentures: immediate tray cleaning, proper cast trimming, and causes of inaccurate or weak casts. It discusses limitations of stock trays and the advantages of individual acrylic-resin/VLC trays, with detailed fabrication techniques for maxillary and mandibular trays, wax spacers, stops, perforations, handling, and polymerization. It also introduces Chapter 16 on distal extension denture base support, including factors influencing support, tooth-supported RPD support from abutments, and impression methods for functional support of distal extension bases.

structure.summary: This section covers impression materials and procedures for removable partial dentures, classifying materials as rigid, thermoplastic, and elastic. It details the properties, indications, handling, advantages, limitations, and precautions for each, emphasizing that elastic materials are preferred for undercuts. It also covers principles for impressions of the partially edentulous arch, including accurate recording of teeth and tissues without permanent deformation, hydrocolloid techniques and cast-making issues, custom acrylic-resin/visible light-cured tray fabrication, and introduces distal extension denture base support considerations.

structure.title: Support for the Distal Extension Denture Base

nodes.title: DISTAL EXTENSION REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURE
nodes.summary: The text covers distal extension removable partial dentures, explaining their reliance on residual ridge support because they lack tooth support at both ends, the importance of indirect retention, and the need to preserve distal abutments or inform patients of limitations if they are absent. It lists six factors influencing residual ridge support and discusses ridge contour and quality, noting that the ideal ridge is rarely found. In the mandible, the crest is not a primary stress-bearing area, while the buccal shelf and ridge slopes provide vertical and horizontal support; in the maxilla, the overlying tissue is generally firmer but topography limits stress-bearing areas. The figure description emphasizes recording the crest, retromolar pads, and lingual slopes undisplaced, while allowing additional pressure on the buccal shelf.

nodes.title: FACTORS INFLUENCING THE SUPPORT OF A DISTAL EXTENSION BASE
Contour and Quality of the Residual Ridge
nodes.summary: The text discusses distal extension removable partial dentures, emphasizing their reliance on the residual ridge for support, stability, and retention. It lists factors influencing residual ridge support, describes ideal and actual ridge characteristics for the mandible and maxilla, stresses the importance of broad denture base coverage, explains anatomic versus functional impression forms, and includes figure descriptions of stress-bearing areas and relief regions.

nodes.title: Extent of Residual Ridge Coverage by the Denture Base
nodes.summary: The text discusses support for distal extension denture bases, emphasizing that the crest of the residual ridge is the primary vertical stress-bearing area, with buccal and lingual slopes providing limited support and counteracting rotation. Displaceable palatal tissues require relief. It stresses maximum residual ridge coverage for better load distribution, the importance of broad denture bases, and the distinction between anatomic and functional ridge forms in impression registration, including materials and factors affecting accuracy. A comparison shows properly extended bases distribute occlusal forces better than underextended ones.

nodes.title: Type and Accuracy of the Impression Registration
nodes.summary: This text discusses principles for supporting distal extension denture bases, focusing on stress-bearing areas, residual ridge coverage, and impression techniques. It emphasizes the crest of the maxillary residual ridge as the primary support, the need for broad base coverage to distribute loads, and the distinction between anatomic and functional ridge forms. It also reviews impression philosophies, functional impressions, Steffel's classification of treatment approaches, and the requirements for either physiologic basing or the use of stress-breakers.

nodes.title: Support for Distal Extension Denture Base: Fit, Framework, and Load
key_items: Accuracy of the Fit of the Denture Base
Design of the Removable Partial Denture Framework
nodes.summary: The page covers support for distal extension denture bases, focusing on accuracy of denture base fit, framework design, and total occlusal load. It emphasizes intimate tissue contact, accurate master-cast reproduction, and proper base-to-framework relationship, especially with the altered cast technique. Framework design involves inevitable rotation under load, greatest movement at the posterior ridge, and benefits of placing occlusal rests more anteriorly to use more residual ridge support, though minor-connector disengagement from the guiding plane is uncertain. Regarding occlusal load, patients tend to chew over natural teeth, so residual ridge support should be optimized and shared; artificial tooth number, width, and occlusal efficiency affect total load, with Kaires's investigation supporting reduction of occlusal surface size.

nodes.title: Total Occlusal Load Applied
nodes.summary: This text covers support for the distal extension denture base, emphasizing fit accuracy, framework design, and rotational movement under load. It discusses how anterior placement of occlusal rests can improve residual ridge support, and how total occlusal load is influenced by patient chewing behavior and artificial tooth form. It explains the limitations of anatomic form impressions, which record resting tissues and can overload abutments and distal bone, and describes the objective of functional impression techniques to maximize base support, minimize movement, and reduce stress on abutment teeth.

The section covers factors influencing support of distal extension denture bases: residual ridge contour and quality, extent of denture base coverage, type and accuracy of impression registration, framework fit and design, and total occlusal load. It emphasizes the residual ridge as the primary support, the need for broad base coverage, the distinction between anatomic and functional impression forms, and the importance of controlling occlusal load to reduce stress on abutment teeth.

nodes.title: ANATOMIC FORM IMPRESSION
nodes.summary: The text covers a figure on occlusal rest and guiding plane preparation for a lower premolar, a quotation about the benefits of a narrowed occlusal table, the limitations of anatomic form impressions for removable partial dentures, the need for functional support and load distribution, differing impression/relining opinions, and the objectives of functional impression techniques for distal extension bases.

nodes.title: METHODS FOR OBTAINING FUNCTIONAL SUPPORT FOR THE DISTAL EXTENSION BASE
Selective Tissue Placement Impression Method
nodes.summary: This chapter discusses support for the distal extension denture base. It explains that a secondary or corrected impression is necessary because no single material records both anatomic and functional forms. The impression method is chosen based on mucosal support potential. The selective tissue placement impression method uses custom trays and controlled tissue displacement to maximize support and avoid tissue damage. The framework must be fitted carefully in the mouth before attaching trays; figure captions illustrate tray fabrication and framework adjustment. The altered cast impression method is commonly used for mandibular Kennedy Class I and II arches, while maxillary arches usually rely on firm palatal support. The selected pressure or dynamic impression method controls material flow to load primary stress-bearing areas. Finally, the functional impression technique is described for uniformly firm mucosa, recording tissue form during occlusion, while the selective pressure method remains applicable to all ridge conditions.

nodes.title: Functional Impression Technique
nodes.summary: The text discusses support for distal extension denture bases, focusing on altered cast and selective-pressure impression techniques for mandibular Kennedy Class I and II arches, as well as the functional impression technique for uniformly firm ridges. It then introduces occlusal relationships for removable partial dentures, emphasizing the fourth treatment phase: establishing a functional, harmonious occlusion while recognizing that RPD occlusion differs from complete denture occlusion due to direct abutment-tooth loading, common causes of occlusal failure, and the need to conform to the existing occlusal pattern.

This section covers methods for obtaining functional support for distal extension denture bases. It begins with an illustrated discussion of occlusal rest and guiding-plane preparation and the limitations of anatomic form impressions, which record tissues at rest and can unevenly distribute masticatory load, overloading distal bone and abutments. The goal of functional impression techniques is to maximize denture base support, maintain occlusal contact, and minimize leverage on abutment teeth. Described methods include selective tissue placement with custom trays and controlled tissue displacement, the altered cast method for mandibular Kennedy Class I and II arches, selected pressure/dynamic impression of primary stress-bearing areas, and functional impression for uniformly firm mucosa. The section also introduces occlusal relationships for RPDs, emphasizing the fourth treatment phase of establishing functional, harmonious occlusion, the differences between RPD and complete denture occlusion, causes of occlusal failure, and conforming to the existing occlusal pattern.

structure.summary: This section covers support for the distal extension denture base, contrasting tooth-supported RPDs with distal extension RPDs. It explains that distal extension bases rely on the residual ridge because they lack distal tooth support, lists six factors influencing base support, and details ridge contour and quality in the mandible and maxilla. It discusses the limitations of anatomic form impressions and the need for functional support, then describes methods for obtaining functional support such as selective tissue placement, the altered cast method, selected pressure/dynamic impression, and functional impression for firm mucosa. Finally, it introduces occlusal relationships for RPDs, including establishing functional occlusion, differences from complete denture occlusion, causes of occlusal failure, and conforming to the existing occlusal pattern.

structure.title: Occlusal Relationships for Removable Partial Dentures

nodes.title: DESIRABLE OCCLUSAL CONTACT RELATIONSHIPS FOR REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES
nodes.summary: The text describes principles and recommended occlusal relationships for removable partial dentures (RPDs). It notes exceptions where complete denture principles apply, otherwise remaining teeth dictate occlusion, with planned centric contacts and no lateral interferences. It outlines the steps for establishing satisfactory occlusion and lists eight specific occlusal arrangements for different RPD types: tooth-supported, distal extension, unilateral, maxillary complete denture opposing, and Kennedy Class IV cases. It also emphasizes the importance of tooth position relative to the residual ridge—avoiding the retromolar pad/upward incline, directing mandibular stress to the buccal shelf, and managing maxillary tipping—for distal extension denture stability.

nodes.title: METHODS FOR ESTABLISHING OCCLUSAL RELATIONSHIPS
Direct Apposition of Casts
nodes.summary: The text discusses establishing jaw relationships for partially edentulous patients. It first outlines four diagnostic conditions that determine whether to fabricate restorations in centric relation or a planned intercuspal position. It then describes two methods: direct apposition of casts, used when opposing teeth allow obvious hand occlusion, and interocclusal records with posterior teeth remaining, used when hand occlusion is not possible. The limitations of wax records are explained, followed by a detailed step-by-step procedure for making and correcting an interocclusal wax record using a metal-reinforced wafer and occlusal registration material to ensure accurate mounting.

nodes.title: Interocclusal Records With Posterior Teeth Remaining
nodes.summary: The text covers establishing occlusal relationships for removable partial dentures. It first lists four pretreatment conditions that determine whether the restoration should be fabricated in centric relation or a planned intercuspal position. It then describes three methods for recording jaw relations: direct apposition of casts for obvious relationships; interocclusal wax records with posterior teeth remaining, including detailed wax record procedures, correction with metallic oxide paste, advantages of the paste, precautions, and conditions for pouring an opposing cast; and occlusion rims on record bases for distal extension or large edentulous situations, including fabrication of visible light-cured and autopolymerizing acrylic-resin record bases. The importance of accurate, stable record bases and the role of occlusion rims in providing posterior support are emphasized.

nodes.title: Occlusal Relations Using Occlusion Rims on Record Bases
nodes.summary: The text discusses methods for recording jaw relations and establishing occlusion for removable partial dentures. It covers the use of opposing casts and metallic oxide paste for interocclusal records, the construction and use of occlusion rims on accurate record bases for cases with edentulous areas or missing opposing contacts, techniques for making VLC and acrylic-resin record bases, requirements for record base accuracy, methods for recording centric relation on record bases, jaw relation records made entirely on occlusion rims when no natural tooth contact exists, and the recording of occlusal pathways using occluding templates. It also emphasizes the importance of accurate bases, proper record materials, dentist skill in final occlusal adjustments, and the role of anterior guidance in occlusal rehabilitation.

nodes.title: Jaw Relation Records and Occlusion Establishment on Record Bases
key_items: Methods for Recording Centric Relation on Record Bases
Jaw Relation Records Made Entirely on Occlusion Rims
nodes.summary: The page covers methods for recording jaw relations and establishing occlusion in removable partial dentures. It first describes record base requirements, materials, and the need for correct ridge-form support and cast compatibility. It then reviews centric relation recording methods on record bases, including wax and modeling plastic rims, hard-setting recording media, and the need for accurate transfer to casts. Next, it explains jaw relation records made entirely on occlusion rims for situations with no opposing natural tooth contacts, such as opposing complete dentures or anterior-only arches. Finally, it discusses establishing occlusion through recorded occlusal pathways with an occluding template, notes the influence of remaining natural teeth, and highlights Schuyler's emphasis on anterior guidance before complete oral rehabilitation.

nodes.title: Establishing Occlusion by the Recording of Occlusal Pathways
nodes.summary: The text covers methods for recording jaw relations and establishing occlusion for removable partial dentures. It describes requirements for accurate record bases, methods for recording centric relation on record bases, jaw relation records made entirely on occlusion rims, and the fifth method using functional registration of occlusal pathways. It emphasizes the influence of remaining natural teeth, canine guidance, the need for a dynamic occlusal concept, diagnostic wax-ups, sequencing when both arches are restored, and a step-by-step procedure for registering occlusal pathways by having the patient wear a wax rim for 24 hours to capture all extremes of mandibular movement.

nodes.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Registering Occlusal Pathways
nodes.summary: This text covers occlusal relationships for removable partial dentures, emphasizing dynamic occlusion and canine guidance, diagnostic wax-ups, sequencing restoration of arches, a detailed step-by-step method for registering occlusal pathways with a wax occlusion rim, conversion to an occluding template, material choices for artificial posterior teeth, principles for arranging teeth to an occluding template, and establishment of jaw relations for a mandibular removable partial denture opposing a maxillary complete denture.

This section covers methods for establishing occlusal relationships for removable partial dentures. It first discusses the need for facebow mounting of the maxillary cast, articulator limitations, and the dominant influence of remaining natural teeth on occlusion. It then describes five methods: direct apposition of casts, interocclusal records with posterior teeth remaining, occlusion rims on record bases, jaw relation records made entirely on occlusion rims, and establishing occlusion by recording occlusal pathways with an occluding template. Key considerations include diagnostic conditions for choosing centric relation or intercuspal position, accurate record base fabrication, use of wax and metallic oxide paste, anterior/canine guidance, and step-by-step procedures for registering mandibular movements.

nodes.title: MATERIALS FOR ARTIFICIAL POSTERIOR TEETH
key_items: Arranging Teeth to an Occluding Template
nodes.summary: The text covers occlusal relationships for removable partial dentures, including the use of stone stops to maintain vertical relation, selection and modification of artificial posterior teeth (acrylic vs. porcelain, gold occlusal surfaces, narrow occlusal forms), arranging teeth to an occluding template with emphasis on functional occlusion and positioning, and establishing jaw relations when a mandibular RPD opposes a maxillary complete denture, including the facebow transfer and impression procedure for an existing maxillary denture.

nodes.title: ESTABLISHING JAW RELATIONS FOR A MANDIBULAR REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURE OPPOSING A MAXILLARY COMPLETE DENTURE
nodes.summary: The text covers occlusal relationships for removable partial dentures: material choices for artificial posterior teeth, arranging teeth to an occluding template, and establishing jaw relations for a mandibular RPD opposing a maxillary complete denture, including existing denture use, concurrent denture construction, tooth-supported versus distal-extension cases, and occlusal correction. It also introduces Chapter 18, listing its laboratory procedure topics and explaining that it focuses specifically on RPD laboratory work, with an initial discussion of duplicating stone casts.

structure.summary: This section covers the establishment of occlusal relationships for removable partial dentures, explaining the importance of occlusal harmony and the influence of remaining natural teeth. It describes desirable occlusal contact patterns for various RPD configurations, methods for recording jaw relations (including direct apposition, interocclusal records, occlusion rims, and occlusal pathway registration), materials and modification of artificial posterior teeth, arranging teeth to an occluding template, and specific procedures for a mandibular RPD opposing a maxillary complete denture. It also addresses common causes of occlusal failure and introduces the laboratory procedures detailed in Chapter 18.

structure.title: Laboratory Procedures

nodes.title: DUPLICATING A STONE CAST
key_items: Duplicating Materials and Flasks; Duplicating Procedure
nodes.summary: This chapter focuses on dental laboratory procedures for removable partial denture fabrication. It begins with duplicating a stone cast for preservation, framework fitting, temporary prostheses, and investment casting, noting materials and the importance of blockout and temperature control. It then outlines waxing the framework, including preformed patterns and freehand waxing, as well as subsequent laboratory steps such as spruing, investing, burnout, casting, finishing, record bases, occlusion rims, occlusal templates, tooth arrangement, acrylic-resin base processing, remounting, occlusal correction, and polishing. The chapter assumes prior knowledge of fixed and complete denture laboratory techniques.

nodes.title: WAXING THE REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURE FRAMEWORK
Forming the Wax Pattern for a Mandibular Class II Removable Partial Denture Framework
nodes.summary: The text covers laboratory procedures for removable partial denture frameworks, including duplication and refractory casts, wax pattern formation, preformed plastic patterns, attaching wrought-wire retainer arms by soldering, and waxing metal bases. It emphasizes framework design communication, quality evaluation, patient comfort, material selection, soldering precautions, and differences in relief requirements for acrylic-resin versus cast metal bases.

nodes.title: Attaching Wrought-Wire Retainer Arms by Soldering
nodes.summary: This text from Part II Clinical and Laboratory discusses maxillary waxed framework examples, preformed plastic patterns and their handling, waxing procedures for various direct retainers and major connectors, soldering attachment of wrought-wire retainer arms, and waxing metal bases including relief considerations for acrylic-resin, complete metal, and partial metal bases. It also references figures and Chapter 12 for related laboratory and alloy information.

nodes.title: Waxing Metal Bases
nodes.summary: The text covers laboratory procedures for removable partial denture frameworks, including a completed maxillary waxed framework example, preformed plastic patterns, waxing of direct retainers and major connectors, soldering wrought-wire retainer arms, and detailed techniques for waxing complete and partial metal bases with attention to relief, borders, boxing, and acrylic-resin retention. Numerous figure captions illustrate mandibular and maxillary wax patterns, framework evaluation, design transfer, clasp configurations, tissue stops, finish lines, and I-bar retainers. The section ends by introducing spruing, investing, burnout, casting, and finishing of the framework, along with Brumfield's factors for casting excellence.

This section covers laboratory procedures for waxing removable partial denture frameworks, including evaluation of frameworks on master casts, cast duplication materials and techniques, formation of wax patterns using preformed plastic patterns and freehand waxing, waxing of direct retainers and major connectors, soldering attachment of wrought-wire retainer arms, and detailed waxing of metal bases with appropriate relief and retention. It also emphasizes the dentist's role in framework design communication, quality evaluation, patient comfort, material selection, soldering precautions, and introduces subsequent steps of spruing, investing, burnout, casting, and finishing.

nodes.title: SPRUING, INVESTING, BURNOUT, CASTING, AND FINISHING OF THE REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURE FRAMEWORK
Spruing
nodes.summary: The text covers laboratory procedures in dental casting, including soldering of wrought-wire retainers, a comprehensive list of factors affecting casting quality, and detailed principles of spruing—such as sprue function, design rules, multiple vs. single sprue configurations, and specific examples for mandibular and maxillary frameworks. It also describes investing procedures, purposes of the investment material, and considerations for alloy types and dimensional compensation.

nodes.title: Investing the Sprued Pattern
nodes.summary: The text covers spruing and investing procedures for removable partial denture castings. It details sprue sizes and configurations for mandibular and maxillary frameworks, single versus multiple spruing, and specific multiple-spruing guidelines. It explains the two-part investment process, the purposes of investment, differences between gold and chromium-cobalt alloy investments, and burnout procedures including mold preparation, oven temperature control, and manufacturer recommendations. Figures illustrate sprued patterns and investment application techniques.

nodes.title: Dental Casting Investments and Burnout Procedure
nodes.summary: The page covers dental casting investments and the burnout procedure. It explains investment materials and expansion for gold and chromium-cobalt alloys, including shrinkage percentages and the need for careful spruing and venting. It describes the step-by-step investing technique, then details burnout: its purposes, preparation steps such as soaking and orientation, furnace placement, temperature guidelines, and manufacturer recommendations. It also includes figure captions showing a sprued wax pattern and brush application of investment.

nodes.title: Casting, Divesting, and Finishing in Dental Lab Procedures
key_items: Removing the Casting From the Investment
nodes.summary: The page covers casting procedures and post-casting finishing in dental laboratory work. It explains casting force methods and regulation, metal melting techniques, and electrically controlled casting machines. It also describes divesting, finishing, electropolishing, and polishing of chromium-cobalt castings, along with recommendations about sprue removal and related figure content.

nodes.title: Finishing and Polishing
nodes.summary: The text covers laboratory procedures for casting dental frameworks, removing castings from investment, finishing and polishing, and making record bases. It describes casting force regulation, melting methods, and modern casting machines; explains divesting and electropolishing of chromium-cobalt alloys; gives finishing and polishing precautions and rules; and discusses materials and techniques for jaw relation record bases, including relining, blockout of undercuts, permanent bases, sprinkled acrylic-resin record bases, and visible light-cured materials.

This section covers the laboratory procedures for producing removable partial denture frameworks, beginning with illustrated features of I-bar retainers, tissue relief and stops, finishing lines, and retention methods (spurs, loops, nailheads) for acrylic resin attachment. It also describes soldering wrought-wire clasps to cast frameworks and Brumfield's factors affecting casting quality. The main procedural topics include spruing principles and configurations for mandibular and maxillary frameworks; investing techniques and investment materials for gold vs. chromium-cobalt alloys; burnout procedures and furnace guidelines; casting methods, force regulation, and melting; and post-casting steps such as divesting, electropolishing, finishing, and polishing. The section concludes with techniques for making jaw relation record bases, including relining, blockout, permanent bases, sprinkled acrylic-resin bases, and visible light-cured materials.

nodes.title: MAKING RECORD BASES
key_items: Technique for Making a Sprinkled Acrylic-Resin Record Base
nodes.summary: The text covers laboratory procedures for finishing frameworks and making jaw relation record bases. It describes framework polishing methods, requirements for record base materials, advantages of processed or cast permanent bases, management of undercuts, and the detailed sprinkled acrylic-resin technique including blockout, monomer/polymer application, polymerization, and accuracy considerations. Visible light-cured bases are also mentioned, and the importance of an accurate, stable record base for jaw relation records is emphasized.

structure.summary: The section covers dental laboratory procedures for removable partial denture fabrication, starting with duplicating a stone cast and waxing the framework. It then details spruing, investing, burnout, casting, finishing, and polishing of the framework, along with retention and soldering techniques. Finally, it describes methods for making record bases, including processed, cast, sprinkled acrylic-resin, and visible light-cured bases, emphasizing accuracy and stability for jaw relation records.

structure.title: OCCLUSION RIMS
structure.summary: The text covers occlusion rims for removable partial dentures: their required accuracy, materials such as wax and modeling plastic, proper shaping, static and functional recording techniques, and the chairside procedure for building functional occlusion rims with inlay wax. It also describes laboratory steps for making a stone occlusal template from a functional occlusal record, including cast keying, framework seating, cleaning, and clay matrix formation.

structure.title: MAKING A STONE OCCLUSAL TEMPLATE FROM A FUNCTIONAL OCCLUSAL RECORD
structure.summary: The text covers laboratory and chairside procedures for establishing functional occlusion in removable partial dentures. It describes using inlay wax occlusion rims, their preparation and chairside adjustment, including establishing height, width, and occlusal vertical dimension. It then details making a stone occlusal template from a functional occlusal record: keying and preparing the cast, cleaning and seating the framework, forming a clay matrix, using vertical stone stops, pouring stone template, mounting on an articulator, and trimming. Finally, it discusses arranging posterior teeth against the opposing cast or template, emphasizing the need for stable acrylic-resin or metal bases and the inappropriateness of tissue-supported record bases for functional records.

structure.title: ARRANGING POSTERIOR TEETH TO AN OPPOSING CAST OR TEMPLATE
key_items: Posterior Tooth Forms; Arranging Teeth to an Occluding Surface
Arranging Teeth to an Occluding Surface
structure.summary: The text covers laboratory procedures for removable partial dentures, including creating an occlusal template and maintaining vertical relation during articulator mounting; preparing and handling record bases and metal frameworks; selecting and modifying posterior tooth forms to harmonize with existing dentition; arranging posterior teeth to opposing casts or templates; and choosing anterior tooth types and managing their esthetic try-in and preservation.

structure.title: TYPES OF ANTERIOR TEETH
structure.summary: The text covers laboratory procedures for removable partial dentures, including handling and reattaching the metal framework, selection and modification of posterior and anterior tooth forms, materials and occlusal considerations, arranging teeth to occlusal surfaces, types of anterior teeth and their advantages/disadvantages, and waxing/investing procedures before acrylic-resin processing. It also discusses finishing-line management, prevention of acrylic-resin seepage, gingival contour waxing for esthetics, and Frush's rules for gingival tissue heights.

structure.title: WAXING AND INVESTING THE REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURE BEFORE PROCESSING ACRYLIC-RESIN BASES
key_items: Waxing the Removable Partial Denture Base
structure.summary: The text covers anterior tooth options for removable partial dentures (cemented facings and resin veneers), then details waxing and investing RPD bases before processing acrylic-resin bases. It includes guidelines for wax contours, gingival esthetics, and papilla formation; flasking and investment techniques to preserve the cast, avoid occlusal changes, and manage framework support; trial packing, land space, and boil-out procedures; and processing with characterization options.

structure.title: PROCESSING THE DENTURE
structure.summary: This text discusses laboratory procedures for removable partial dentures: flasking, packing acrylic resins (trial and no-trial), land-space creation, investing, boil out, separating media, framework support, denture base processing and characterization, ideal base material properties, the Success Injection System and VLC denture base materials, considerations for dimensional accuracy and future materials, and the need for remounting/occlusal correction with specific remounting precautions.

structure.title: REMOUNTING AND OCCLUSAL CORRECTION TO AN OCCLUSAL TEMPLATE
key_items: Precautions to Be Taken in Remounting
structure.summary: The text covers laboratory procedures for removable partial dentures, beginning with the step-by-step handling of a VLC denture base, followed by a brief discussion of denture base material limitations and future requirements. It then details remounting and occlusal correction, including the necessity of remounting after processing, the precautions required for accurate remounting, and methods for occlusal reshaping and tooth adjustment. It also describes remounting of completed prostheses using new records and remounting casts. Finally, it addresses denture polishing, emphasizing proper border management, facial and lingual surface contouring, and modern gingival/interproximal finishing techniques.

structure.title: POLISHING THE DENTURE
structure.summary: The text covers two main topics: denture polishing and work authorizations for removable partial dentures. It describes polishing considerations for denture borders, facial surfaces, and gingival/interproximal areas, emphasizing accurate impressions, proper border extension, wax contouring, careful finishing to avoid a denture look, and safety hazards during lathe polishing. It also introduces work authorizations, their purpose, required contents, and their role in providing instructions and quality assurance for laboratory fabrication.

structure.title: Work Authorizations for Removable Partial Dentures

nodes.title: WORK AUTHORIZATION
nodes.summary: The text discusses work authorizations for removable partial dentures, defining them as written directives for laboratory work that ensure quality, legal protection, and clear communication between dentist and technician. It lists required content, four key functions, and essential characteristics such as clarity and comprehensiveness. It emphasizes that separate forms are needed for different laboratory stages and types of prostheses, and shows that well-designed forms can efficiently provide detailed instructions, as demonstrated in a completed example.

nodes.title: DEFINITIVE INSTRUCTIONS BY WORK AUTHORIZATIONS
nodes.summary: The text covers the purpose and design of work authorizations for removable partial dentures, including efficient form layouts, material selection, diagrams, color codes, waxing specifications, and clear instructions. It also discusses legal and regulatory aspects, the need for duplicate records, and the delineation of responsibilities: the dentist remains fully responsible for the prosthodontic service, while the laboratory technician is responsible only to the dentist, and improper delegation or poor communication can lead to legal and professional problems.

nodes.title: LEGAL ASPECTS OF WORK AUTHORIZATIONS
nodes.summary: The text covers the content and purpose of work authorization forms for removable partial dentures, including materials selection, tooth selection, diagrams, color-coding of master casts, waxing specifications, and duplicate copies. It also discusses the legal aspects of work authorizations, state regulations, record retention, and the delineation of responsibilities between dentists and laboratory technicians, emphasizing that the dentist remains ultimately responsible and that poor instructions or improper delegation can lead to illegal practice and conflicts.

nodes.title: DELINEATION OF RESPONSIBILITIES BY WORK AUTHORIZATIONS
nodes.summary: The text discusses work authorizations for removable partial dentures, covering their content, material specifications, tooth selection, diagrams, color-coding, waxing specifications, legal requirements, and the delineation of responsibilities between dentist and laboratory technician. It emphasizes clear communication, ethical delegation, and avoiding illegal or inferior practice. It then introduces the initial placement and servicing of removable partial dentures, stressing scheduled insertion, necessary adjustments, occlusal harmony, patient education, and the dual meaning of adjustment.

structure.summary: The section covers work authorizations for removable partial dentures, including their definition, required content, functions, characteristics, and the need for separate forms for different stages and prostheses. It details form design aspects such as materials, tooth selection, diagrams, color-coding, waxing specifications, and duplicate copies. It also addresses legal and regulatory considerations, record retention, and the delineation of responsibilities: the dentist is ultimately responsible, while the laboratory technician is responsible only to the dentist, and improper delegation is illegal. Finally, it introduces the initial placement and servicing of removable partial dentures, emphasizing scheduled insertion, adjustments, occlusal harmony, patient education, and the dual meaning of adjustment.

structure.title: Initial Placement, Adjustment, and Servicing of the Removable Partial Denture

nodes.title: ADJUSTMENTS TO BEARING SURFACES OF DENTURE BASES
nodes.summary: The text describes final laboratory and clinical adjustments required for prosthetic dentures. It emphasizes perfecting occlusion and denture base contours, adjusting denture bearing surfaces using pressure indicator paste to identify and relieve pressure areas, and addressing common pressure zones in both arches. It also covers the need to eliminate occlusal interference from denture frameworks and stresses the importance of trying the framework in the mouth before final delivery to avoid patient trauma.

nodes.title: OCCLUSAL INTERFERENCE FROM DENTURE FRAMEWORK
nodes.summary: The text covers the initial placement, adjustment, and servicing of removable partial dentures. It emphasizes perfecting occlusion between artificial and natural dentition, finishing denture bases, and using pressure indicator paste to identify and relieve pressure areas on bearing surfaces, including common pressure locations and special considerations like xerostomia. It also discusses eliminating occlusal interference from the metal framework, the need to try the framework in the mouth before finishing, and final occlusal adjustments to harmonize with natural occlusion in all mandibular positions. Figure 20-1 is described, demonstrating appropriate paste application, placement techniques, and interpretation of pressure patterns.

nodes.title: ADJUSTMENT OF OCCLUSION IN HARMONY WITH NATURAL AND ARTIFICIAL DENTITION
nodes.summary: This text covers initial placement and adjustment of removable partial dentures. It describes use of pressure indicator paste to detect and relieve tissue-surface pressure, principles and techniques for occlusal adjustment to harmonize with natural dentition, the advantage of articulator-based remount procedures for distal extension dentures, a sequence for adjusting opposing RPDs, intraoral indicators and occlusal wax methods, restoration of occlusal anatomy after adjustment, the need for repeated and periodic occlusal rechecks, and patient instructions for prosthesis insertion, removal, and monitoring.

nodes.title: INSTRUCTIONS TO THE PATIENT
nodes.summary: The text covers occlusal adjustment of removable partial dentures, including methods using indicator wax, marking and relieving excessive contacts, adjusting chewing-stroke interferences, restoring occlusal anatomy, and scheduling follow-up adjustments and periodic rechecks. It provides detailed patient instructions on denture placement and removal, managing expectations about discomfort, phonetics, bulk reduction, oral hygiene, cleaning products, nighttime wear, and the 24-hour recall appointment. Follow-up services emphasize periodic recalls, recognizing and correcting loss of ridge support, proper clasp retention adjustments, and patient rules to prevent damage and caries.

nodes.title: FOLLOW-UP SERVICES
nodes.summary: The text covers post-placement care, adjustment, and servicing of removable partial dentures, including night-use precautions, the need for a 24-hour follow-up appointment, proper clasp retention adjustment, detection of ridge support loss, and patient instructions for denture maintenance and prevention of caries and periodontal damage. It also introduces relining and rebasing of RPDs, defining both procedures, describing impression methods and materials, choosing closed- vs open-mouth techniques based on mucosal resiliency, and emphasizing the need for healthy oral tissues before the procedure.

structure.summary: This section covers the initial placement, adjustment, and follow-up servicing of removable partial dentures. It emphasizes that insertion is a scheduled essential phase and that patients should not be dismissed until denture bases are adjusted, occlusal discrepancies are corrected, and patient education is completed. Adjustment is described as both dentist-performed denture surface corrections and patient accommodation. Technical content includes perfecting denture base contours and occlusion, using pressure indicator paste to identify and relieve pressure areas and common pressure zones, eliminating framework occlusal interference, trying the framework before delivery, harmonizing occlusion with natural dentition in all mandibular positions, managing xerostomia, remount procedures for distal extension bases, adjusting opposing RPDs, using intraoral indicators and occlusal wax, restoring occlusal anatomy, and performing periodic occlusal rechecks. Patient instructions address insertion/removal, expectations, phonetics, bulk reduction, oral hygiene, cleaning products, nighttime wear, the 24-hour recall, and monitoring. Follow-up services include periodic recalls, detecting loss of ridge support, adjusting clasp retention, preventing damage and caries, and relining/rebasing with impression methods and closed- vs open-mouth considerations based on mucosal resiliency and healthy tissue status.

structure.title: Relining and Rebasing the Removable Partial Denture

nodes.title: RELINING TOOTH-SUPPORTED DENTURE BASES
nodes.summary: The text discusses relining and rebasing removable partial dentures, covering the use of existing denture bases for reline impressions, management of tissue abuse, indications and limitations for tooth-supported bases, metal base considerations, closed-mouth impression techniques, direct reline procedures with autopolymerizing resin including detailed steps and precautions, and the special considerations for distal extension bases, including the need for periodic evaluation and relining.

nodes.title: RELINING DISTAL EXTENSION DENTURE BASES
nodes.summary: The text covers relining and rebasing of removable partial dentures, focusing on direct reline materials and technique, indications for relining distal extension bases, patient education, diagnosis using occlusal contact and rotation tests, the open-mouth reline impression procedure, conditions for success, and the beginning of a discussion on reestablishing occlusion after relining.

nodes.title: METHODS OF REESTABLISHING OCCLUSION ON A RELINED REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURE
nodes.summary: The text covers maintenance and relining of removable partial dentures, including indications for relining distal extension bases (loss of occlusal contact and rotation due to loss of tissue support), the open-mouth relining impression technique to maintain framework position, conditions for successful reline, methods for reestablishing occlusion using remount casts and restoring resin or replacing teeth, and the beginning of repairs and additions, focusing on minimizing repair needs and causes/prevention of broken clasp arms.

structure.summary: This section covers relining and rebasing of removable partial dentures. It distinguishes relining (resurfacing the tissue side of the denture base) from rebasing (replacing the entire denture base), noting that relining is more common. Both require a new impression using the existing denture base as a modified tray, with open-mouth or closed-mouth techniques and various impression materials. The choice of technique depends on tooth support versus distal extension bases, particularly mucosal resiliency, and framework movement must be prevented. Tissue health must be restored before the procedure. The section details relining tooth-supported bases, including direct reline procedures with autopolymerizing resin and metal base considerations; relining distal extension bases, including indications, diagnosis via occlusal contact and rotation tests, patient education, and the open-mouth reline impression technique; and methods of reestablishing occlusion after relining using remount casts and restoring resin or replacing teeth. It also introduces repairs and additions, emphasizing minimizing repair needs and preventing broken clasp arms.

structure.title: Repairs and Additions to Removable Partial Dentures

nodes.title: BROKEN CLASP ARMS
nodes.summary: The text introduces repairs and additions to removable partial dentures, emphasizing that these should be uncommon with proper diagnosis, treatment planning, and fabrication. It outlines the chapter topics, discusses patient education to prevent damage, and focuses in detail on broken clasp arms: their causes, prevention, and repair options. A figure illustrates repair of a fractured canine retainer with a wrought-wire arm and highlights the need to evaluate whether the denture is still serviceable.

nodes.title: FRACTURED OCCLUSAL RESTS
nodes.summary: The text covers repair of fractured occlusal rests and distortion or breakage of major/minor connectors in removable partial dentures. It explains causes, especially inadequate rest seat preparation for occlusal rests and patient abuse or adjustment-weakening for connectors, and describes soldering repair techniques, including impression-making, platinum foil adaptation, electric soldering with gold solder or industrial brazing alloy, and the need for adequate metal bulk and careful handling.

nodes.title: DISTORTION OR BREAKAGE OF OTHER COMPONENTS—MAJOR AND MINOR CONNECTORS
nodes.summary: The chapter covers repairs and additions to removable partial dentures: causes and soldering repair of fractured occlusal rests; management of distorted or broken major/minor connectors, including when to remake rather than adjust; addition of teeth to resin or metal bases and relining considerations; replacement of lost abutment teeth with new direct retainers; miscellaneous repairs of prosthetic teeth and resin bases; and electric soldering techniques, including solder selection, flux use, and procedural steps.

nodes.title: Maintenance of Removable Partial Dentures: Repairs and Soldering
key_items: LOSS OF A TOOTH OR TEETH NOT INVOLVED IN SUPPORT OR RETENTION OF THE RESTORATION
LOSS OF AN ABUTMENT TOOTH NECESSITATING ITS REPLACEMENT AND MAKING A NEW DIRECT RETAINER
nodes.summary: The text covers maintenance and repair of removable partial dentures, addressing when to remake versus repair: faulty survey/design/fabrication or tissue impingement calls for remaking, and repeated adjustments causing connector failure may require a new restoration or soldered replacement. It describes adding teeth to resin and metal bases, relining after base extension, replacing a lost abutment with an adjacent tooth prepared to the original path, and other repairs such as replacing teeth or repairing resin bases. It also details soldering techniques, including electric soldering, appropriate gold solders and fluxes for gold and chromium-cobalt alloys, and the use of platinum foil as a backing/trough during the procedure.

nodes.title: REPAIR BY SOLDERING
nodes.summary: The text covers repairs and additions to removable partial dentures and introduces interim removable partial dentures. It explains when failed castings must be remade, how to handle tooth loss and abutment loss, various repairs, and detailed electric and torch soldering procedures with appropriate alloys, fluxes, and heat treatment. It also lists the indications, fabrication methods, retention options, and patient considerations for interim RPDs, including a figure example of repairing a fractured lateral incisor prosthesis.

structure.summary: The section covers repairs and additions to removable partial dentures, emphasizing prevention and proper initial treatment. It details repair of broken clasp arms, fractured occlusal rests, and distorted or broken major and minor connectors, including soldering techniques and when remaking is preferable. It also addresses adding teeth to resin or metal bases, relining, replacing lost abutment teeth with new retainers, miscellaneous repairs of teeth and resin bases, and the use of interim removable partial dentures.

structure.title: Interim Removable Partial Dentures

nodes.title: APPEARANCE
nodes.summary: The text discusses interim removable partial dentures: their purpose as temporary prostheses within a total treatment plan, materials and retention methods, patient warnings, and six clinical indications. It details two specific uses—appearance restoration and space maintenance—including fabrication techniques, design considerations, and age-related rationale for maintaining spaces after tooth loss.

nodes.title: SPACE MAINTENANCE
nodes.summary: The text discusses maintenance in prosthodontics, focusing on interim removable partial dentures and space maintenance. It describes two clinical cases: one involving an interim mandibular prosthesis with specific flange designs to improve lip activity, and another involving maxillary anterior extractions where an interim prosthesis provides esthetics and stabilization. It also explains the importance of maintaining edentulous spaces after tooth loss, with different considerations for younger patients (until abutment/implant readiness) and adults (to prevent tooth migration and extrusion until definitive treatment).

nodes.title: Interim Removable Partial Dentures: Uses, Conditioning, and Treatment
nodes.summary: The page covers interim removable partial dentures: their use in reestablishing occlusion, conditioning teeth and residual ridges, serving as occlusal splints, supporting distal extension bases, and providing temporary restorations during treatment. It also describes modifying existing dentures, replacing teeth with interim prostheses, and preparing patients for complete dentures.

nodes.title: CONDITIONING THE PATIENT FOR WEARING A PROSTHESIS
nodes.summary: The text discusses interim removable partial dentures, covering their purposes in establishing occlusal relationships and conditioning teeth and ridges, their use as occlusal splints, modification of existing dentures during treatment, patient transition to complete dentures, and clinical placement procedures. It emphasizes proper fit, adjustment, blockout, and occlusal harmony to ensure comfort, stability, and tissue health before definitive prosthetic treatment.

nodes.title: CLINICAL PROCEDURE FOR PLACEMENT
nodes.summary: The text discusses interim/transitional removable partial dentures: their role as temporary restorations when further treatment of natural teeth is impractical, conditions for providing them, and the clinical procedure for placement, including seating, adjustments, blockout, occlusal considerations, and avoidance of over-reliance on the prosthesis for occlusion. It then introduces Chapter 24 on removable partial denture considerations in maxillofacial prosthetics, outlining topics such as maxillofacial classification, timing of care, design for maxillary and mandibular defects, maxillary and mandibular prostheses, and jaw relation records, and explaining how maxillofacial patients differ due to altered oral anatomy and reduced support, stability, and retention.

structure.summary: The section covers interim removable partial dentures as temporary prostheses within a comprehensive treatment plan, including materials, retention methods, patient warnings, and six clinical indications. It details their use in appearance restoration and space maintenance, with fabrication/design considerations and clinical cases, as well as their roles in reestablishing occlusion, conditioning teeth and ridges, serving as occlusal splints, supporting distal extension bases, and providing temporary restorations. The text also addresses modifying existing dentures, preparing patients for complete dentures, conditioning the patient for wearing a prosthesis, and the clinical placement procedure with fit, adjustment, blockout, and occlusal harmony. It concludes by introducing removable partial denture considerations in maxillofacial prosthetics, emphasizing differences due to altered oral anatomy and reduced support, stability, and retention.

structure.title: Removable Partial Denture Considerations in Maxillofacial Prosthetics

nodes.title: MAXILLOFACIAL PROSTHETICS
nodes.summary: The text covers removable partial denture considerations in maxillofacial prosthetics, including the unique challenges posed by surgical resections, trauma, congenital defects, developmental anomalies, and neuromuscular disease. It describes classification of maxillofacial defects and prostheses, timing of prosthetic care for acquired defects, intraoral prosthesis design principles, surgical preservation for prosthesis benefit, types of maxillary and mandibular prostheses, mandibular resection classifications, and jaw relation records for mandibular resection patients.

nodes.title: TIMING OF DENTAL AND MAXILLOFACIAL PROSTHETIC CARE FOR ACQUIRED DEFECTS
Preoperative and Intraoperative Care
nodes.summary: This text discusses removable partial denture considerations in maxillofacial prosthetics, covering classification of maxillofacial defects as acquired, congenital, or developmental, and classification of prostheses by location, duration, and purpose. It outlines a care timeline for acquired defects, emphasizing preoperative and intraoperative care to manage dental disease, preserve strategically important teeth, take impressions, and plan prosthetic treatment, along with interim care focused on surgical management. The text also notes that mandibular discontinuity defects are rarely surgical outcomes today, though the discussion is incomplete.

nodes.title: Interim Care
nodes.summary: The text covers maxillofacial prosthetic care, including preoperative consultation and its psychological/functional benefits, management of dental disease before surgery, use of presurgical impressions and planning, interim prosthetic care for maxillary defects, surgical obturators and interim prostheses, support and retention challenges with large defects, and potential complications during the transition from active treatment to observation.

nodes.title: Potential Complications
nodes.summary: This text covers maxillofacial prosthetic management after maxillary resection, focusing on the interim and definitive phases. It describes maxillary defect types and interim obturator prostheses, then details potential complications such as discomfort, retention problems, leakage, and chemo/radiation effects. It explains sources of prosthetic discomfort, retention strategies using clasps or adhesives, prosthesis adjustments during healing, and swallowing instructions. Oral and defect hygiene practices are emphasized, including cleaning methods, fluoride use, and periodontal management. Finally, it discusses definitive prosthetic care, reasons for delay, and the importance of avoiding prolonged temporary prostheses to achieve full rehabilitation.

nodes.title: Defect and Oral Hygiene
nodes.summary: The text covers maintenance phases of maxillofacial prosthetic care. It discusses interim prosthesis adjustments after surgery, including managing changes in fit, speech, swallowing, and leakage, with strategies such as temporary liners and specific patient instructions. It addresses complications from radiation and chemotherapy, especially mucositis and long-term effects like xerostomia and osteoradionecrosis. Defect and oral hygiene are emphasized, including cleaning techniques, management of secretions and debris, and preventive measures such as fluoride for high-risk patients. Finally, the text describes the transition to definitive prosthetic care once tissues mature, reasons for delays, and the importance of providing complete rehabilitation rather than overusing temporary prostheses.

nodes.title: Definitive Care
nodes.summary: The text covers maintenance and definitive care of maxillofacial prostheses, especially obturators. It discusses interim prosthesis adjustments after surgery, managing leakage and swallowing, complications like mucositis and xerostomia, and the importance of defect hygiene and oral care. Definitive prosthetic management is described as a later transition after tissue maturation, with design differences from interim prostheses. The text also addresses principles of removable partial denture design in maxillofacial prosthetics, including support/stability mechanisms, design goals, and surgical preservation considerations for maxillary defects, with prostheses such as obturators and speech aids restoring oral-nasal separation and function.

The section covers the timing of dental and maxillofacial prosthetic care for acquired defects, from preoperative and intraoperative planning through interim and definitive phases. It emphasizes early management of dental disease, preservation of strategic teeth, presurgical impressions, and prosthetic treatment planning. Interim care includes surgical obturators and interim prostheses, with attention to support, retention, adjustments during healing, and complications such as discomfort, leakage, and radiation/chemotherapy effects. Hygiene of the defect and oral cavity, fluoride use, and periodontal management are highlighted. Definitive prosthetic care is described as occurring after tissue maturation, with different design principles from interim prostheses, emphasizing full rehabilitation and avoiding prolonged use of temporary devices. The text also covers classification of defects and prostheses, removable partial denture design principles, and restoration of oral-nasal separation with obturators and speech aids.

nodes.title: INTRAORAL PROSTHESES: DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS
nodes.summary: The text discusses removable partial denture considerations in maxillofacial prosthetics, focusing on the functional limitations of prostheses, the importance of surgical defect characteristics and patient skill, design goals and strategies for intraoral prostheses, support mechanisms related to remaining teeth and mucosa, and surgical preservation principles for maxillary defects—emphasizing restoration of oral-nasal separation and use of obturator and speech aid prostheses.

nodes.title: SURGICAL PRESERVATION FOR PROSTHESIS BENEFIT
Maxillary Defects
nodes.summary: The text discusses removable partial denture considerations in maxillofacial prosthetics, emphasizing that surgical defect characteristics, reconstruction choices, and remaining teeth critically influence prosthesis success. It contrasts definitive and interim obturators, outlines prosthetic design goals and support mechanisms, and details surgical preservation strategies for maxillary and mandibular defects. Key topics include tooth preservation and resection techniques, soft palate management, split-thickness skin grafting, defect extension requirements, indications for surgical reconstruction, palatal augmentation for tongue defects, and the importance of soft tissue reconstruction that preserves tongue mobility. Overall, the goal is to achieve functional restoration without compromising tumor control.

nodes.title: Mandibular Defects
nodes.summary: The text discusses surgical versus prosthetic management of maxillary and mandibular defects in maxillofacial prosthetics. For maxillary defects, surgery is appropriate only for small defects that can be reconstructed without compromising function or prosthetics; otherwise prosthetic rehabilitation is preferred, especially for soft palate defects. Mandibular defects require careful surgical planning to preserve continuity, soft tissue mobility, and function. Reconstruction with plates maintains contour but limits tooth replacement; bone graft techniques and implants have improved outcomes. The ideal reconstructed mandible should provide stable union, facial contour, adequate attached mucosa, and functional sulci.

nodes.title: Mandibular Reconstruction—Bone Grafts
nodes.summary: The text discusses removable partial denture considerations in maxillofacial prosthetics. It covers the functional and cosmetic consequences of mandibular resection, the importance of maintaining mandibular continuity, use of reconstruction plates, and mandibular reconstruction via bone grafts and flaps, including ideal ridge characteristics, implant considerations, and complications.
